layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Biden approved nuclear strategy to focus on China

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Classified plan scrutinizes its growing arsenal

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
By David E. Sanger  
NEW YORK TIMES

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: President Biden approved in March a highly classified nuclear strategic plan for the United States that, for the first time, reorients America's deterrent strategy to focus on China's rapid expansion in its nuclear arsenal.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The shift comes as the Pentagon believes China's stockpiles will rival the size and diversity of the United States' and Russia's over the next decade.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The White House never announced that Biden had approved the revised strategy, called the "Nuclear Employment Guidance," which also seeks, for the first time, to prepare the United States for possible coordinated nuclear challenges from China, Russia, and North Korea. The document is so highly classified that there are no electronic copies, only a small number of hard copies distributed to a select few national security officials and Pentagon commanders.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But in recent speeches, two administration officials were allowed to allude to the change - in carefully constrained sentences - ahead of a more detailed, unclassified notification to Congress expected before Biden leaves office.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The president recently issued updated nuclear-weapons employment guidance to account for multiple nuclear-armed adversaries, Vipin Narang, a nuclear strategist at MIT who served in the Pentagon, said this month before returning to academia. "And in particular," he added, the weapons guidance accounted for "the significant increase in the size and diversity" of China's nuclear arsenal.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In June, the National Security Council's senior director for arms control and nonproliferation, Pranay Vaddi, also referred to the document, the first to examine in detailo whether the United States is prepared to respond to nuclear crises that break out simulta-

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: neously or sequentially, with a combination of nuclear and molecular weapons.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The new strategy emphasizes "the need to deter Russia, the PRC, and North Korea simultaneously", Vaddi said, using the acronym for the People's Republic of China.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In the past, the likelihood that American adversaries could coordinate nuclear threats to outmaneuver the American nuclear arsenal seemed remote. But the emerging partnership between Russia and China and the conventional arms North Korea and Russia is likely to bring to Russia for the war in Ukraine have fundamentally changed Washington's thinking.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The new document is a reminder that whoever is sworn in next Jan. 20 will confront a changed and far more volatile nuclear landscape than the one that existed just three years ago. President Vladimir Putin of Russia has threatened the use of nuclear weapons against Ukraine, including during a crisis in October 2022, when Biden, looking at intercepts of conversations between Russian commanders, feared the likelihood of nuclear use might rise to 50 percent or higher.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden, along with leaders of Germany and Britain, got China and India to make public statements that there was no roles for the use of nuclear weapons in Ukraine, and the crisis abated temporarily.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It was an important moment," Richard N. Haas, a former senior State Department and National Security Council official for several presidents, and the president emeritus of the Council on Foreign Relations, noted in an interview. "It is not clear why Russia that is radicalized; this idea that nukes would not be used in a conventional conflict is not longer a safe assumption."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The second big change arises from China's nuclear ambitions. The country's nuclear expansion is running at an even faster pace than American intelligence officials anticipated when it was given the power by President Xi Jinping's determination to scrap the decades-long strategy of maintaining a "minimum deterrent."

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: War draining Ukraine's male workforce

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: FINBARR O'REILLY/NEW YORK TIMES/FIELE

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: A Ukrainian woman recently waited with colleagues for an elevator to the surface of a mine run by steelmaker Metinvest.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Women heed call to fill roles once off limits

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: By Constant Meheut NEW YORK TIMES

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: PAVLOHRAD, Ukraine  On a recent morning in eastern Ukraine, Karina Yatsina, a mine worker, was busy operating a conveyor belt in a dim, 1,200- square meter. Lights flickered at the end of the shaft, illuminating miners carving out the coal seams.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A year and a half ago, Yatsina, 21, was working as a nanny. Then friends told her that a mine in the eastern town of Pavlohrad was hiring women to replace men drafted into the military. The pay was good and the pension generous. It wasn't long before Yatsina was walking through the mine's maze of tunnels, a headlamp strapped to her red helmet.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I would have never thought that I would be working in a mine," Yatsina said, taking a short break in the sweltering heat of the tunnel. "I would have never imagined that."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Yatsina is one of 130 women who have started working underground at the mine since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. They now operate conveyors that carry coal to the surface, work as safety inspectors, or drive the trains that connect the different parts of the mine.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Their help is enormous" said Serhiy Faraonov, deputy head of the mine, which is run by DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company. About 1,000 male workers at the mine have been drafted, he said, or about a fifth of the total workforce. The mine has hired some 330 women.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: They are part of a wider trend in Ukraine, where women are increasingly stepping into jobs long dominated by men. They have become truck or bus drivers, welders in steel factories and shopkeepers, and house workers. Thousands have also voluntarily joined the army.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In doing so, these women are reshaping Ukraine's traditionally male-dominated work-

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: force, which experts say has long been marked by biases inherited from the Soviet Union. "There was this perception of women as second-class and less-reliable workers," said Hily Vybinyuk, a senior director of the Kyiv-based Center for Economic Strategy.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Vyshlinsky said that Ukrainian women had long been excluded from certain jobs, not only over physical demands but also because such roles were considered too complicated for them. Women, he said, could drive trolley buses, but not trains. "It was full of stereotypes."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The current influx of women into the Ukrainian job market has echoes of the munitionettes, the British women who worked in arms factories during World War I, and the women - memorialized in the iconic posters of Rosie the Riveter - who went

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: to work in the United States during World War II.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But even with the influx of women into the workforce, they will not be enough to replace all the male workers who have left, economists say. Three-quarters of Ukrainian employers have experienced labor shortages, a recent survey showed.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Before the war, 47 percent of Ukrainian women worked, according to the World Bank. Since then, some 1.5 million female workers have been about 13 percent of the total, have left Ukraine, Vryshlyinskiy said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: “The share of women cur-rently working in Ukraine is higher than before the war,” Vyshlinsky said. But too many have left Ukraine to allow the country to overcome its workforce shortages, he said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The phenomenon of women joining the workforce has been particularly evident in the min

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: ing industry.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: After Russia invaded in 2022, the Ukrainian government suspended a law that had barred women from working underground and in "harmful or dangerous" conditions. Now, they are a regular presence in the cramped lift shafts that take workers to the depths of the mines.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I was surprised. It's unusual to see a woman with a shovel doing a man's work," said Dmytro Tobalov, a 28-year-old miner, not long after a woman walked past him and other burly miners who were resting on benches in a tunnel, waiting to board the elevator back out of the mine.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Tobalov, who works at a mine in Pokrosk, in the eastern Donetsk region, said 12 men had left his group of miners for the army, replaced by 10 men and two women. "They're doing

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: great," he said of the women.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Several women said they had joined the Pokrovsk mine, owned by Metinvest, Ukraine's largest steelmaker, because it offered stable jobs in a war-ravaged economy. Valentyna Korotaeva, 30, a former shop assistant in Pokrovsk, said she lost her job after a Russian missile attack on the mine, causing the owner to pick up and leave. She now works as a crane operator at the mine, moving large metal machines under repair in a warehouse.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: How long Korotavae can keep her job will depend on the situation on the front line, just 8 miles from the mine. Russian forces have been creeping closer to Pokrovsk in recent weeks. Russia still relies on the sea, sea, and the mine's management has prepared evacuation plans in case it becomes too dangerous to remain there.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Israel says it recovered bodies of 6 hostages

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: THE HOSTAGES FAMILIES FORUM VIA ASSOCIATED PRESS

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Six undated photos of Israeli hostages from top left: Alexander Cyad, Avraham Munder, and Yagev Buchshtab; from bottom left, Yoram Metzger, Haim Peri, and Nadav Popplewels.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Noted they were retrieved from tunnel in Gaza

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: By Isabel Kershner NEW YORK TIMES

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: JERUSALEM - Israel forces recovered the bodies of six Israel hostages from the southern Gaza Strip in an overnight operation, the Israeli military said Tuesday, highlighting the plight of the scores of captives fleeing in the Palestinian en-clave. Five of the six were previously known to have lost their lives.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Of the roughly 250 people Israeli authorities say were taken hostage during the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attack, Israeli forces have so far rescued only seven hostages alive. Scores of others, mostly women and children, were returned to Israel during a weeklong cease-fire in November. More than 100 captives still remain in Gaza, at least 30 of whom are believed to be dead.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant said the six bodies had been retrieved from Hamas tunnels beneath the city of Khan Younis in a “complex op-eration,” and the military re-leased their names.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Avraham Munder, 79, was the only hostage among the six whose death had not already been established. He was abducted from Nir Oz, a kibbutz, or communal village, near the Gaza border, along with three of the others: Haim Peri, 80; Yoram Metzger, 80; and Alexander Dancyc, 75. The remaining two, Nadav Popplewell, 51, and Yagev Buchstab, 35, were taken from another border community, Nirm.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The exact circumstances of their deaths were not immediately clear. Abu Ubaida, a spokesperson for Hamas's military wing, said in March that Metzger and Peri were among seven hostages who had been killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza. The former said in May that Potembele had died from injuries sustained in an Israeli airstrike more than a month before.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Weeks later, the Israeli military said it was examining the possibility that the three hostages had been killed while Israeli forces were operating in the Khan Younis area.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: On Tuesday, the military said the operation to extricate the six bodies came after prolonged combat in a built-up area. The

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: military said Israeli forces found a 30-foot-deep tunnel shaft that led to an underground route, along which they neutralized obstructions, blast doors, weapons, explosives, and militants' hideouts, the statement said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The military said Israel forces scanned the route and noticed that part of the tunnel's concrete lining was loose. When soldiers removed the lining, they discovered a hidden branch of the tunnel network and found the bodies.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A spokesperson for the Israe-li military, Lieutenant Colonel Nadav Shoshani, said the tun-nel was under an area previous-ly designated as part of the hu-manitarian zone of Khan You-nis. The Israeli military has

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: shrunk that zone repeatedly as it presses its assault.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The retrieval of the bodies came as US Secretary of State Antony Blinken continued a diplomatic push in the region for a cease-fire deal that would see hostages released in exchange for Palestinian prisoners held in Israel. Frustration has grown in Israel over the months of halting negotiations, and family members of the hostages still in Gaza have led regular protests demanding a deal to secure their freedom.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has blamed Hamas for obstructing a deal. His critics in Israel, as well as Hamas officials, say that Netanyahu recently added new conditions to a proposal outlined by

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: President Biden in late May, adding to the difficulty of finalizing a deal.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Our hearts grieve over the terrible loss," Netanyahu said in a statement Tuesday following the military's announcement about the retrieval of the bodies. "The state of Israel will continue to work hard to return all of our hostages - the living and the deceased."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: On Tuesday, Blinken ended his ninth visit to the Middle East since the war in Gaza began without securing any major breakthrough for deal, warning that "time is of the essence."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: After meetings in fellow mediating countries, Egypt and Qatar, Blinken said that because Israel has accepted a proposal to bridge gaps with the militant group the focus turns to doing everything possible to "get Hamas on board" and ensure both sides agree to key details on implementation.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "We need to get a cease-fire and hostage agreement over the finish line, and we need to do it now. Time is of the essence," he said before leaving Qatar.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: said before leaving Qatar. There has been added urgency after the recent targeted killings of militant leaders of Hamas and Hezbollah in Iran and Lebanon, both attributed to Israel, and vows of retaliation that have sparked fears of a wild

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Few details have been released about the bridging proposal put forth by the United States, Egypt, and Qatar. Blinken said it is "very clear on the schedule and the locations of [Israeli military] withdrawals from Gaza."

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Accused serial killer escapes custody in Kenya

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: LONDON - Kenyan authorities have launched a search for a suspected serial killer who escaped from custody after being accused of killing scores of 10, the national police said Tuesday.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: And, police said, he probably had help.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Our preliminary investigations indicate that the escape was aided by insiders," Gilbert Masengeli, an inspector general, said in a statement Tuesday. He said the actions of eight officers were on duty at the time of the escape were being investigated.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Kenyan police arrested the suspect, Collins Jumaisi Khaslusa, in July after dismembered bodies were discovered at an abandoned quarry in Nairobi. They said he had confessed to having killed 42 women over the past two years.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: On Tuesday, Khalusha escaped from his cell in the Gigiri police station in Nairobi, police said, fleeing along with 12 Eritreans who had been accused of being in Kenya illegally. The police station is near the US Embassy, a United Nations office, and other diplomatic missions.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Panama deports 29 Colombians on US-paid flight

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: PANAMA CITY — Panama deported 29 Colombians on Tuesday on a flight that the government said was the first paid admission to the United States under an agreement the two countries signed in July.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Colombians had entered Panama illegally through the Darien Gap, a path used by more than 500,000 migrants last year. The vast majority of those were Mexicans.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: For now, Panama is not able to deport Venezuelans because the relationship between the two countries turned tense after Panama-like most other countries in the region-refused to recognize the results of Venezuela's election giving President Nicolás Maduro another term. The two countries have suspended their diplomatic relations.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: President José Raúl Mulino of Panama, who took office July 1, pledged to stop that migration flow, an interest he shares with the US government.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Mulino had originally said the flights would be "voluntary" repatriations, but those deported Tuesday had criminal records, officials said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: ASSOCIATED PRESS

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Mexico judges vote to strike with court staff

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: MEXICO CITY - Federal judges voted Monday night to go on strike across Mexico, protesting President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador's proposed overhaul of the country's judicial system. The judges will join thousands of union employees who went on indefinite strike earlier in the day over the contentious policy changes.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The moves reflect rising tensions over López Obrador's push for the most sweeping changes to Mexico's legal system in decades. He and his supporters want thousands of Mexico's judges, including those on the Supreme Court, to be required for an election instead of being appointed based on qualifications and specialized training.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: López Obrador has defended the plan, arguing that its goal is to rid the judiciary of “corruption and privileges." Critics say the change could result in people with minimal legal experience being elected to judgeships.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The vote to strike means that on Wednesday, more than 1,400 judges and magistrates will join the federal court workers who walked off the job Monday.

layout_dets.text:
By Peter Baker  
NEW YORK TIMES

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: CHICAGO-When the crowd members in the United Center first chanted, "Thank

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: NEWS ANALYSIS

layout_dets.label: 段落

you, Joe! Thank you, Joe!"  
Monday night, President Biden

layout_dets.text: But he knew. He might not have wanted to admit it. But he knew. They were thanking him, yes, for what he accomplished during a lifetime in public service. But they were also thanking him for not running again.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: As much as they cheered

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden and waned their preprinted "We [Love] Joe" signs, the thousands of Democrats gathered for their quadrennial national convention were sending him off to the presidential retirement home four years before he was ready. Biden found himself demoted from speaking as the presidential nominee on Thursday night, when as recently as a month ago he had expected to address the convention, to Monday night, an evening usually reserved for the party's past stars.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden, 81, gave little indication that he was eager to go. While he made a couple of self-deprecating jokes about his age, he barely alluded to his decision to step aside under pressure from fellow Democrats worried that the most richest president in the nation's history would sink the party. When he did, he simply framed it as an act of sacrifice to save American democracy from former presi

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: dent Donald Trump.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It's been the honor of my lifetime to serve as your president," he said in a 52-minute speech capping the first night of a convention celebrating the nomination of Vice President Kamala Harris to be his successor. "I love the job, but I love my country more. I love my country more than I ever did this talk about what I'm angry at all the people who said I should step down - it's not true."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: At that point, the crowd chanted, "We love Joel!"

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I love my country more,” Biden repeated, "and we need to preserve our democracy."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Citing song lyrics, he offered a valedictory. "America, America, I gave my best to you," he said. "I made a lot of mistakes in my career. Well, I gave my best to you for 50 years. Like many of you, I've given my heart and soul to our nation, and I've been blessed a million times in return with the support of the Ameri

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: can people."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: He might not acknowledge being angry, but he was not going out of his way to offer forgiveness either. After leaving the hall, he spoke briefly to reporters at the airport before leaving on Air Force One for a vacation in California and was asked about his relationship with former House speaker Nancy Pelosi, who was seen as a critical force in pressing him out of the race. “No, I haven’t spoken to her,” he said, then added, “No one made my decision but me.”

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: This was the 13th convention that Biden attended going back to 1972 and at least the eighth where he spoke, but the last he would address as a current office holder or candidate — to give one speech he never wanted to deliver. He has been such a part of the American political firmament for so long that it seemed hard to imagine him ceding the spotlight.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: And in fact, he made little ac

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: commodation to that unhappy reality, largely giving what seemed like the speech that could have been written before his withdrawal from the race on July 21, extolling his record and excoriating Trump's.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Indeed, while he declared that picking Harris was the "best decision I made my whole career" and praised her as "tough" and "experienced with 'enormous power," he did not offer an extended term to her, leaving that to future speakers on future nights.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: After he wrapped up his speech, though, Harris appeared onstage to honor him. "I love you so much," she could be seen telling him as she hugged him. Looking up at him as if he were her father, she repeated, "I love you."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But the Democrats jumbled their homage plan with a slate of speeches that went so long that Biden was pushed out of prime time on the East Coast. He did

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: not begin his own address until about 11:30 p.m. in Washington, a cardinal sin in modern convention planning.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden did not cut short his own address. He had a lot to say and wanted to say it. Much of it was Joe Biden Classic, all the familiar themes, hokey stories, family sayings, unabashed patriotism, and sometimes debatable remarks. Some of it adopted the language of "the people" as almost a most word for word, down to the "veins bulging" description of white supremacists marching in Charlottesville, Va., in 2017.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: He finished with the lines he uses to end almost every speech, the paean to American exceptionalism and optimism. "Folks, we just have to remember who we are," he said, raising his voice to a shout. "We're the United States of America, and there's nothing we cannot do when we do it together. God bless you all. And may God protect our troops."

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: CLOSE CONNECTION

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Obama, Harris share a long bond and a kindred spirit

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: KENNY HOLSTON/NEW YORK TIMES

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Former president Barack Obama and Vice President Kamala Harris at a 2022 event commemorating the Affordable Care Act.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She backed him early in '08 race; he didn't forget

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
By Katie Rogers  
NEW YORK TIKES

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: CHICAGO - On New Year's Eve in 2007, Kamala Harris, then the district attorney of San Francisco, prepared to spend the holiday more than 1,000 miles away from her native California. She had flown to Iowa for the first time, touching down in Des Moines during one of the wettest winters on record.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Harris turned up in a dingy campaign field office, wearing a puffy coat and boots. Near a tangle of power cords, someone had propped an "African Americans for Obama" poster against a wall. In the midst of that bleak Midwestern winter, Harris was there to knock on doors for Barack Obama, the junior senator from Illinois mounting a long-shot bid for the presidency.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "To be here is worth 1,000 Champagne bottles and firecrackers," Harris told a reporter on New Year's Day, surrounded by campaign detritus. "It's equal to that, in terms of the thrill, the excitement, and the promise for tomorrow."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Supporting Obama was a po-litical risk. Harris was one of the rare Californians holding elected office — and one of few in the Democratic Party writ large — to

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: endorse him for the presidency. Most of the party’s institutional heft had been thrown behind Hillary Clinton, a senator from New York who had a powerful surrogate in her husband, for-mer president Bill Clinton.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But Harris's early bet paid off, and Obama has not forgotten it.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: “She was just a rock-solid supporter of the president at a time the entire political establishment was not with him,” said Buffy Wicks, a California State Assembly member who was the 32nd person hired by Obama’s campaign. “She set aside significant time and energy to help get him elected, and that was greatly appreciated by him.”

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: On Tuesday evening at the Democratic National Convention, Obama will return the favor. The two share a view of politics that is defined by offering economic and social opportunities to people who have been historically cut off from them.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: “It is a sense that politics is not about you,” said Dan Pfeiffer, who served as a senior adviser to Obama. “It’s about building a movement.”

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: After Obama clinched the Democratic presidential nomination in June 2008 and the presidency that November, Harris surfed a tide of flattering headlines and favorable comparisons to the party's new leader. She declared a run for attorney general of California shortly after Obama was sworn in.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "There's an Obama halo that, you know, he shined the light on her," said Brian Brokaw, ran who ran her campaign for attorney general. "The comparisons came naturally and fast."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Back then, Obama thought she was "smart as hell," he would remark to his aides, praising her abilities as a political performer and her toughness as she waged her unlikely campaign to become California's top law enforcer. But it was not until she had unquestionably become the bigger star, and her support of his campaign took her only so far.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: He did not endorse her until after she won the primary race. For a president to support a candidate in a down-ballot state

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: race would have been unusual, but even after winning, she had to ask for the endorsement, Brokaw recalled.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Still, when Harris visited the White House, she was received "with open arms" by Obama, recalled Wicks, who worked in the Obama administration as deputy director of the White House office of public engagement."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "They met, they clicked, and they have over the years developed a very close friendship," said Valerie Jarrett, one of the most closest friends and a senior adviser to him when he was president.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Both are mixed-race Americans, born to parents who came from different parts of the

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: world, a shared experience that led them both "to believe you can find something in common with just about anybody."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Their shared brand of politics is based on the idea that the ascent of people with racial and cultural backgrounds like theirs, is a testament  to the country's strengths, rather than a rejection of its values.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: They have spent their careers making the case to a predominantly white country that "a skinny kid with a funny name," as Obama called himself as a Senate candidate at the 2004 Democratic convention, and Harris, "a daughter of Oakland" raised in Berkeley, Calif., by a single mother, could help Ameri

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: cans build cultural bridges to one another and transcend political differences.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: When President Biden made the decision to end his 2024 campaign and informed the vice president, she had a round of calls to make. The first several went to family members. But out of more than 100 people the vice president called for a national day, Barack Obama was third or fourth on her list, according to a person briefed on her calls.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "They're both really joyful, optimistic spirits," said Jarrett, who flew with Obama from Martha's Vineyard, to the convention in Chicago on Monday. "That's something they were born with. That hasn't changed over time."

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: FASHION AND A STATEMENT

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: The DNC might feature a lot of white pantsuits. It's not just fashion.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: NEW YORK TIMES/FIL

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Nancy Pelosi and others wore white at President Donald Trump's State of the Union address in February 2019.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: By Tal Kopan GLOBE STAFF

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: WASHINGTON - President Biden had just announced he was leaving the race and the Virginia Democratic convention delegation's group chat exploded with messages. After it quickly became clear that Vice President Kamala Harris would likely be a candidate, someone threw out an idea: What if they all were to wear white suits? The night of her speech at the convention?

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The message of the outfit was clear to everyone in the chat-it would be a nod to Harris's historic candidacy, a throwback to Hillary Clinton's, and a clear contrast with former president Donald Trump. The suggestion that he immediately accepted, ed, said one of the delegates, Sandy Marks, a local party chair in the state.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The significance of the white pantsuit is not simply about fashion. It has become a symbol of modern politics since 2016, when Clinton wore one to accept the Democratic nomination for president as a nod to the suffragettes who wore white as they fought for women's right to vote.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: After her loss, it became a sign of resistance to Trump.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: And this week at the convention, its presence will be a visual marker of how much has changed in national politics over the last eight years - as well as the last four weeks.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Fashion is an absolute language; it's a universal language, said theo tyson, curator of fashion arts at the Museum of Fine Arts Boston. "It's,what is that garment, what is that thing that can unify and communicate, very succinctly, very loudly - but also very quietly, very subtly."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The white outfit has a political history going back over a century. Barrier-breaking women politicians have turned to white outfits on momentous occasions for decades. Shirley Chisholm wore white in 1969 when she was sworn in as the first African American woman elected to Congress, and Geraldine Ferraro did the same in 1984 to accept the vice presidential nomination as the first woman on a major party presidential ticket.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Clinton wore white to Trump's inauguration. House Democratic women, notably then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: si, were the color to his 2019 State of the Union address. Harris herself donned a white suit in 2020 when she gave her acceptance speech as the first woman elected vice president.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Clinton reprised the white suit Monday as she delivered a speech extolling Harris as a continuation of the women's rights legacy she advanced in 2016.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: It's an outfit that almost certainly would not have made an appearance before the events of the past month, when Biden stepped aside and endorsed Harris.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The decision transformed the presidential race from a plodding rematch between two older white candidates who both seemed to turn off voters into a campaign pitting a historic, newer generation candidate in Harris against Trump. The role of gender has taken on outsize importance in the new contest - and not just by virtue of Harris's identity. The contrast has been heightened by the dominance of abortion rights as an issue in the election and amid a slew of comments from Trump and his running mate, Ohio Senator JD Vance, that have de

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: meamed women and Harris's background.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: White clothing has also been adopted by Republican women at key moments, including rightwing firebrand Marjorie Taylor Greene, who wore an all-white ensemble with fur trim when she heckled Biden at his State of the Union address, and Trump's daughters Ivanka and Tiffany, who were dressed in the color onstage with him at the Republican National Convention.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: It's unclear if Harris will re

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: turn to the color for her Thursday night acceptance speech, but the crowd at the DNC will likely be dressed that way regardless. In addition to Virginia's delegation, the Democrats' women's caucus recently urged its membership to wear white on Thursday for Harris's speech.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "That statement of having a number of people on the convention floor flooding it with one single, unifying color, and in this case it being white, is incredibly momentous," said Joanna Rosholm, a former press secretary to first lady Michelle Obama, who compared it to sports fans opening up to games in their team colors. "A lot of it will be people seeing it in their feeds later, and that visual, a flood of support, unifying support for the person on stage, is a really powerful visual."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Fashion and culture writer Tom Fitzgerald, of the blog Tom and Lorenzo, hopes Harris will choose something other than the white pant suit for her speech, saying it is too associated in his mind with Clinton and her loss in 2016.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It is a powerful symbol - I complete understand why any

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: female politician would want to utilize that symbol," Fitzgerald said. "It feels like a response to the Trump years, and with [Harris], even though she is running against Trump, I feel we have a chance here to... put all those symbols behind us."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Harris has her own collection of iconography. Her supporters often use the catchphrase "Chucks and pearls," a reference to her habit of wearing Chuck Taylor Converse sneakers (which she collects) for casual occasions around the world, such as the wear of pearl necklaces. Indeed, Chuck Taylors were ubiquitous at the convention in many forms.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: And as a sign of unity on the convention floor, tyson said, a fashion statement makes perfect sense as a political statement.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "You think about all of the different jobs we have and industries and geographies we live in.... It might be the one thing you can do to use your voice," tyson said, "to don a white suit, or to put on a string of pearls, or to grab a pair of Chucks, and that serves as your resistance."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Tal Kopan can be reached at tal.kopan@globe.com.

layout_dets.label: 页眉
layout_dets.text: WEDNESDAY, AUGUST 21, 2024

layout_dets.label: 页眉
layout_dets.text: THE BOSTON GLOBE

layout_dets.label: 页眉
layout_dets.text: The Nation

layout_dets.label: 页码
layout_dets.text: A5

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Obamas leading the charge for Democrats

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: EVA HAMBACH/AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: ANDREW HARNIK/GETTY IMAGES

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Delegates gathered at the United Center in Chicago. Former President Barack Obama took aim at Donald Trump, accusing him of whining about his problems.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: DEMOCRATS

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Continued from Page A1

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: a broad coalition in her bid to defeat Trump this fall. She is drawing on stars like the Obamas and other celebrities, officials from the far left to the middle, and even some Republicans to boost her campaign.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: And while the theme of the night was "a bold vision for America's future," the disparate factions of Harris's evolving coalition demonstrated, above all, that they are connected by a deep desire to prevent a second Trump presidency.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Just ahead of the Obama's remarks, Harris addressed an estimated 15,000 people in battleground Wisconsin in the arena where Republicans held their convention last month. She declared that she is running "a people-powered campaign."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Together we will chart a new way forward," the vice president said in remarks that were partially broadcast to the DNC. "A future for freedom, opportunity, and justice, of optimism, and faith."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Back in Chicago, Senators Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, and Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent beloved by progressives, both praised Harris. And in an appearance perhaps intended to needle Trump, his former press secretary Stephanie Grisham — now a harsh critic of her former boss — also took the convention stage.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Trump "has no empathy, no morals, and no fidelity to the truth," Grisham said. "I love my country more than my party. Kamala Harris tells the truth. She respects the American people. And she has my vote."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Still, it was not all serious on the second night of the four-day convention.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A symbolic roll call in which delegates pledged their support for the Democratic nominee turned into a party atmosphere. A DJ played a mix of state-specific songs – and Atlanta native LJJ Jon ran out during Georgia's turn to his hit song with DJ Snake, “Turn Down for What,” to the delight of the thousands inside the cavernous United Center.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Second gentleman Doug Emhoff, who would become the nation's first gentleman if his wife wins the presidency,

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: shared personal details about his relationship with Harris - their cooking habits, their first date, and her laugh, which is often mocked by Republican critics.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "You know that laugh. I love that laugh!" Emhoff said as the crowd cheered. Later, he added,

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Her empathy is her strength."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Trump, meanwhile, was out on the campaign trail as part of his weeklong swing-state tour during the Democratic convention. He went to Howell, Mich., on Tuesday and stood aside sheriff's deputies as he labeled Harris the "ringleader" of a

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Marxist attack on law enforcement" across the country.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Kamala Harris will deliver crime, chaos, destruction, and death," Trump said in one of many generalizations about an America under Harris.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Harris, meanwhile, cast the election in dire, almost existen

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: tial terms. She implored Americans not to get complacent in light of the Supreme Court decision carving out broad presidential immunity, a power she said Trump would abuse.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She has also seized on Trump’s opposition to a nationally guaranteed right to abor

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: tion.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "They seemingly don't trust women," she said of Trump and his Republican allies. "Well, we trust women."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The vice president's speech evoked some of the same themes that underlay Biden's case for reelection before he dropped out, casting Trump as a threat to democracy. Harris said that he is threatening the values and freedoms that Americans hold dear.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Trump said he would be a dictator only on his first day in office, a quip he later said was a joke, and has vowed as president to assert more control over federal prosecutions, an area of power that has traditionally been left to the Justice Department.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Someone with that record "should never again have the opportunity to stand behind the seal of the president of the United States," Harris said. "Never again."

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Harris loyalists from 2020 say it's the party that's evolved

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: CHIP SOMODEVILLA/GETTY IMAGES

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Rapper Lil Jon performed with the Georgia delegation during the ceremonial roll call.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: DELEGATES

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Continued from Page A1

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: the background of her rise to the top of the ticket. While Harris assumed the nomination through a desperate transfer of power, not a primary, supporters new and old insist the biggest difference now is not that she simply happened to be next in line.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In Chicago, Democrats see a candidate who has grown as a leader since a bruising primary and a tumultuous stretch as vice president. But they also see a party - and, they hope, an electorate - more ready to support her.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "She hasn't truly changed in any magnificent, life-altering way," said Felicia Martin, a Wisconsin delegate from Milwaukee who supported Biden in the 2020 primary. "We as the electoral body have been exposed to her, seeing her a little bit more. Now that she's on our radar, we're paying a little bit more attention, so now we have a better feeling of who she is and what she's about. This thing about, 'Oh, she's evolved'— no, we've evolved. Our thinking of her has evolved."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Many Democrats are gushing about Harris now that she has replaced President Biden as the Democratic nominee. A Chicago convention that some were dreading has, with Harris's rise, turned not just into a coronation but a celebration of a potentially history-making president and new generational leader in the party.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Like others within the small contingent of day-one Harris supporters in Chicago, however, Ghosh wasn't preoccupied with other matters where all the energy and enthusiasm were four years ago.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I'm just glad they're here

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: with us," she said in a hallway packed with Harris converts. That sentiment was repeated almost verbatim by another 2020 Harris supporter, Dusty Kirk, at a Monday breakfast for Pennsylvania's delegation.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Denise Glennon, a 2020 Harris supporter, recalled how the candidate's sharp attacks in primary debates four years ago turned some Democrats off.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She came up as a prosecutor, so in the debate, she came out kind of like, really hard," Glennon said. "For some people, she wasn't as relatable."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Republicans, who have spent years mocking Harris's missteps and setbacks, have reacted to her swift embrace with skepticism that she is a changed candidate. They see a party desperate for an alternative to a fading Biden that mobilized around the only viable option - and one who has so far not faced tough questions from the press as the Democratic nominee.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Nothing I've seen is different from her 2019 presidential campaign yet," said Matt Gorman, a Republican strategist who advised Senator Tim Scott's presidential campaign. "She was very impressive in scripted settings. She gave a great announcement speech, but when she got into spontaneous scenarios she suffered. She has yet to be in those much yet, but her trying to explain how she'll pay for her economic plan was painful."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But to Democrats who have followed Harris's career closely, she has made specific strides to become truly ready for this presidential campaign.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In April 2023, Republicans in the Tennessee legislature sparked national outrage when they voted on expelling three

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Democratic members who protested gun violence in the capitol, Harris quickly flew to Nashville and gave a well-received speech inside a chapel at a historically Black university.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Californian who cochaired Vermont Independent Senator Bernie Sanders' 2020 campaign, said her actions in Nashville that night showed she had "found her voice."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Representative James Clyburn, the influential South Carolina Democrat who famously helped clinch his state for Biden in 2020, also identified that speech as a key moment. "The speech she gave that night, I'm

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: sitting there and right in the middle [of] that speech, I said, 'She has arrived,' " Clyburn said. Tuesday at a convention panel hosted by Axios.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The other key moment in Harris's evolution, according to Democrats, was her role in leading the Biden administration's advocacy on abortion rights after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Earlier this year, she embarked on what the White House called a "nationwide reproductive freedoms tour" to counter "extreme attacks" on abortion access.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: At those events, Khanna said, People saw that she was looking more and more presidential in

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: those appearances, and she had found her voice."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Admirers of Harris believed she had those qualities on display in 2020, even if they did not translate into a successful campaign.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Emily Cain, a former state senator from Maine, recalled Harris's performance at a debate in Miami in 2019, where she memorably went after Biden over his work with pro-segregation senators and invoked her own experience with desegregation busing. "She was ready then —I was ready for her," said Cain, who could not endorse at the time because of her role in the Democratic women's organiza-

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: tion Emily's List.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Several delegates agreed the Democratic Party is not the same as it was during the 2020 primary, when liberal and moderate factions clashed over policy and pressured candidates to take clear positions on fault-line issues like Medicare For All. Harris often seemed caught between the left and center during those fights, never fully trusted by either side.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Now, the ambiguity is not hurting Harris, nor are her well-documented pivots to the middle on issues such as immigration. Angela Romero, the minority leader in the Utah House who identifies as a "Bernie Sanders Democrat,"said that what "Harris does for me as our presidential nominee is, I'm very progressive, and I think she centers me."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Where you find the commonality is in the middle and sometimes things aren't happen [ing] as fast as I want them to—I think she brings this center to us that provides a balance," Romero said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: For as much as Harris's failed first bid loomed over her vice presidency and contributed to doubts about her replacing Biden on the 2024 ticket, Democrats can now look back to 2020 and see not a moment to forget but the beginning of a next step.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Oftentimes, we think we know what we want, and we really don't know until the opportunity is before us and it's like, standing right there in front of us all along," said Martin, the Wisconsin delegate. "And that's Kamala Harris."

layout_dets.label: 脚注
layout_dets.text: Tal Kopan of the Globe staff contributed to this story. Sam Brodey can be reached at sam.brodey@globe.com.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Kennedy running mate says they may endorse Trump

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s running mate said in a podcast interview that they were considering dropping their struggling independent presidential bid and endorsing Republican candidate Donald Trump, blaming the Democratic Party for what she said was a "sabotage" of their campaign.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In a nearly hourlong interview posted online Tuesday, Nicole Shanaahan, a Silicon Valley investor who has poured more than $10 million into the Kennedy campaign, appeared to concede that their effort was not likely to win victory. The campaign is running out of money; its poll numbers are falling, and its efforts to secure ballot access across all 50 states have hit repeated snags.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "There's two options that we're looking at," Shahnahan said. "One is staying in," hoping to get 5 percent of the vote to establish a viable political party that will have more access to money and be able to get onto election ballots in 2028.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But we run the risk of a Kamala Harris and Walz presidency, as we draw votes from Trump - we draw somehow

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: more votes from Trump."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She continued: "Or we walk away, right now, and join forces with Donald Trump, and we walk away from that and explain to our base why we are making this decision. Not easy."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In response to a request for comment, Stefanie Spear, a spokesperson for the Kennedy campaign, sent a link to a message that Kennedy posted on the social platform X on Tuesday, which read, in part: "As always, I am willing to talk with leaders of any political party to further the goals I have served for 40 years in my career and in this campaign."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Shanahan is a former donor to the Democratic Party who was once married to Sergey Brin, a cofounder of Google. In the podcast interview, she said she was "so disappointed" that she had previously supported the party.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "We wanted to win, we want ed a fair shot," Shanahan said of their presidential bid.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "The DNC made that impossible for us." She accused the Democratic Party of "planting insiders into our campaign to disrupt it and create actual legal issues for us."

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: New York's top court upholds mail-in ballot law

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: ALBANY, N.Y. - A New York law allowing all registered voters to cast their ballots by mail was upheld Tuesday by the state's highest court, which rejected a Republican challenge to the legislation.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The 6-1 ruling from the Court of Appeals affirmed lower courts in finding that the voting expansion law approved by the Legislature last year did not violate the state's constitution. The lawsuit was part of a GOP effort to tighten voting rules after the 2020 election and was led by US Representative Elise Stefanik.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Challengers argued the state constitution mandates that most people vote in person. Chief Judge Rowan Wilson wrote in the majority opinion that while the question was "difficult" and only one person had never considered before, there was no such requirement.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The decision means that the millions of New Yorkers expected to vote in the Nov. 5 election will be able to cast ballots by mail if they wish, something very few people could do before a series of rule changes that began during the pandemic.

layout_dets.label: 段落

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Putin visits Chechnya 3 weeks into incursion

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Special forces train in republic

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: ASSOCIATED PRESS

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: MOSCOW - Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday made an unscheduled trip to Chechnya, a mainly Muslim republic within the Russian Federation, his first visit in nearly 13 years, as Ukraine's stunning cross-border incursion into western Russia entered its third week.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Putin was greeted by Chechnya's self-styled strongman leader, Ramzan Kadyrov, before visiting a special forces academy bearing his own name and speaking with volunteer fighters who train there prior to being deployed in Ukraine.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Putin praised the volunteers and said that as long as Russia has men like them, it will be "invincible," according to reports by Russian state agencies.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Kadyrov said in a post on his official Telegram channels that more than47,000 fighters, including volunteers, have trained at the facility since Moscow began what it terms its "special military operation" in Ukraine.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Fighters from Chechnya, whose bid for independence after the Soviet Union's collapse led to years of war with Russian forces, are participating in both sides of the conflict in Ukraine.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: VYACHESLAV PROKOFYEV/AFP

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: President Vladimir Putin was greeted by the head of the Chechen Republic, Ramzan Kadyrov, upon arrival at Grozny airport.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Pro-Kyiv volunteers loyal to Dzhokhar Dudayev, the late Chechen pro-independence leader, are the sworn enemies of Chechen forces who back Putin and Kadyrov. The latter joined Russia in the monthslong siege of Ukraine's key port of Mariupol and other flashpoints in the country's south and east.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Also on Tuesday, Putin visited the grave of Kadyrov's father, former Chechen leader Akhmat Kadyrov, a command post, and a mosque in the local capital, Grozny.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Kremlin has relied on Kadyrov to keep the North Caucasus stable following years of turmoil. International rights groups have accused Kadyrov's security forces of extrajudicial killings, torture, and abductions of dissenters, but Russian authorities have stonewalled demands for investigations.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Kremlin scrambled fighters from Chechnya to help protect Moscow from an abortive mutiny launched by mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin last year, but some commentators warned that Kadyrov's ambitions could also potentially pose a threat to federal authorities.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: As of Tuesday evening, neither the Kremlin nor Kadyrov shared any details about the purpose and timing of Putin's unexpected visit, with Kadyrov saying only that "a busy schedule" awaited the Russian leader.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Putin later that evening held talks with Kadyrov at the Chechen leader's residence in Grozny.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Earlier that day, Putin had his first meeting in nearly two decades with mothers of children killed in the 2004 school attack by Islamic militants in Beslan, a town in the Caucasus province of North Ossetia, that left more than 330 people dead.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: At the meeting, he slammed Kyiv's incursion into Russia's Kursk region, accusing the Ukrainians of "trying to destabilize" the country and comparing them to terrorists.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "We will punish the criminals," he said.

layout_dets.text: MICHAEL G. SEAMANS FOR THE BOSTON GLOBE

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Megan Vozzella, whose husband, Stephen, was slain, embraced attorney Benjamin Gideon after the press conference Tuesday.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: MASS SHOOTING

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Continued from Page A1

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: than a road map forward. Any accountability and legal changes will likely be decided through impending lawsuits.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "The investigation has now been completed, and we, on behalf of the families, feel that the next step in this process needs to be real accountability, and that's where we come in," said attorney Benjamin Gideon, who along with Travis Brennan represents about 90 shooting survivors and victims' families.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Standing on the Lewiston City Hall steps after the commission released its report, the pair said they expect to file lawsuits in the coming months.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Commission chair Daniel E. Wathen, former chief justice of the Maine Supreme Judicial Court, said the panel's job was to create a detailed, clear timeline and body of facts to serve as the official record. It's up to politicians and the courts, he said, to act.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "We found the facts, and from those facts, people will draw their own conclusions," Wathen said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Maine Governor Janet Mills, who appointed the commission in November, said in a statement that she "will offer my views to the people of Maine after I have been interviewed and evaluated [the report]."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Many details in the new report had already been made public through media reports, government records, and testimony during the commission's 16 public meetings over the past nine months. The final report from the commission, which had subpoena power and says it used a "procedural review" down of Card's descent into psychosis and levels pointed new criticism at the Army Reserve.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The unit "failed to undertake necessary steps to reduce the threat he posed to the public," the commission wrote. "His commanding officers were well aware of his auditory hallucinations, increasingly aggressive behavior, collection of guns, and ominous comments about his intentions."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Army said in a statement

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: it is "committed to reviewing the findings and implementing sound changes to prevent tragedies like this from recurring." A spokesperson noted an internal investigation led to discipline against three officers in Card's chain of command, as well as a new training procedure to have commanding officers become involved when soldiers are not complying with mentalhealth treatment.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Even with limited information from the Army Reserve, the commission found the Sagadahoc County Sheriff's Office had sufficient probable cause to take Card into protective custody and remove his weapons under Maine's "yellow flag law" about one month before the shooting.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Around 7 p.m. on Oct. 25, a cheerful night at two popular gathering places in Lewiston devolved into scenes of horror

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: when Card, 40 of Bowdoin, opened fire with a semiautomatic rifle on patrons of Schemengees Bar & Grille and the Just-In-Time Recreation bowling alley. Card was found nearly two days later in Lisbon, dead from a self-inflicted gunshot.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Card had experienced a rapid decline in his mental health in the months before the massacre. His family, friends, and colleagues were informed about his increasingly erratic behavior, anger, and paranoia.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In May2023, Card's teenage son and ex-wife alerted police about Card becoming angry at an irrational belief that people were calling him a pedophile and said he had just picked up as many as15 guns from his brother's house, authorities have said. The Sagadahoc County Sheriff's Office passed along the warnings to Card's Reserve unit,

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: based in Saco, but did not make contact with him.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The following July, Card joined his unit in New York to help train West Point cadets. But his erratic behavior led Card's commander, Captain Jeremy Reamer, to order him to undergo an evaluation at the Keller Army Community Hospital at West Point. There, staff recommended he be admitted to the Four Winds psychiatric hospital in Katonah, N.Y.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: While at Four Winds, he showed symptoms of psychosis and "homicidal ideations" and told staff he had a "hit list," according to an Army Reserve report on the shooting released in July.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Staff tried to have him involuntarily committed by a state court, but instead, his Aug. 2, 2023, court date was canceled and Card left the facility the following day, according to the Re

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: serve. The Four Winds physician who treated Card told the commission that "given Card's progress in treatment, his agreement to continue his medications and participate in therapy and his stabilization at that point in time, she did not feel that the hospital would be successful in court," the final report said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Four Winds did not respond to Globe questions Tuesday.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: When he was released, the hospital psychiatrist talked about "the need to see that the firearms were removed from Card's home," according to the commission's final report. She called a doctor at the Army hospital and asked him to file a petition to have his weapons removed under a New York state law.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: None was ever filed, the report found, because local authorities believed the New York law could not apply to the Maine resi

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: dent. That, the report found, was a misunderstanding of the law. Nevertheless, the Four Winds' discharge summary for Card, which was sent to the Keller Army Community Hospital, "indicated that Keller personnel completed" the petition for seizure of his weapons to the state, according to the commission.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Staff at both hospitals recommended Card's personal weapons be secured. Card wasn't allowed access to military weapons while on duty, but Reamer has said he didn't have the authority to seize Card's personal weapons.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: As the first anniversary of the shooting approaches, memorials to the victims still dot the landscape in Lewiston, including outside the bowling alley, which has reopened, and the restaurant, which remains closed.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Megan Vozzella, whose husband, Stephen M. Vozzella, was killed at Schemengees, said Tuesday that more needs to be done to make sure those involved are held accountable and to prevent future violence.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "People are crying out for help, and they're not getting it and the result is that they harm innocent people in innocent communities," Vozzella said. Her shoulder bears a tattoo with her husbands's name under a heart with wings and the words "In loving memory."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: As was her husband, Vozzella is a member of the area's deaf community, and she spoke through an interpreter. Several people killed at the bar were playing in a cornhole league for the deaf community.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Shooting survivor Richard Morlock, who also spoke through an interpreter, said people who lived through the attack support one another, have fun and can still play cornhole. But it's difficult.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I've lost some friends, hearing and deaf friends, and it's a loss," Morlock said. "It's a terrible loss."

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: From a Black family’s lost story, a connection emerges

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: GLOBE STAFF PHOTO ILLUSTRATION

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text:
FROM THE JURY VERDICT:  
In the Case depending between Brom and Bett Plaintiffs against 'John Ashley Esq. Defendant the Jury find that the said Brom and Bett are not and were not, at the time of the purchase of the original Writ, the legal Negro Servants of the said 'John Ashley during Life, and [assess] thirty shillings damages.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Court of Common Pleas, Berkshire, Record Books and File Papers, 1781, Brom and Bett v. Ashley (Judicial Archives, Archives of the Commonwealth, Boston)

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: SLAVERY

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Continued from Page A1

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: chusetts celebrate Aug. 21, the day of the trial in which the jury ruled in Freeman's favor. But three's an air of hope surrounding the day this year.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Finding one of Freeman's descendants felt like a miracle. Genealogical breakthroughs over the past decade have helped African American historians and genealogists build out the Freeman family tree, but sheer luck connected the final branch to Shipperson. Now, such discoveries could have an impact on reparations discussions, which have renewed in recent years across the country as people seek to address the harm inflicted over centuries on descendants of slavery.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: It is unclear whether a fleshed-out family tree could mean monetary compensation for Freeman's descendants. But knowing your family history after generations of the broken family bonds slavery caused, historians say, is repair itself.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "The fact that it is harder [to do African American genealogy] is a legacy of slavery itself," said Kendra Field, an associate professor of history at Tufts University. "It takes more work, it takes time, and investment, and it's the work of repairing those erasurens and voids."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Freeman's life is better documented than most enslaved people of her era. Her headstone suggests she was born around 1744. Known then simply as "Bett," she was owned by Dutch landowner Peter Hogoboom in Claverack, N.Y., during her earlier years. Then in a move that would reverberate down the years, she was moved to Massachusetts. She died down of Sheffield in the Berkshire's to work under Hogoboom's daughter, Hannah, and her husband, Colonel John Ashley, as an enslaved domestic servant.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In 1781, Freeman filed a freedom suit against Ashley. Theodore Sedgwick, a prominent Stockbridge lawyer, and Connecticut attorney Tapping Reeve represented her in court. Be

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: cause Freeman was a woman, she couldn't sue alone. She was joined by a man named Broom whom Ashley also enslaved.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A jury ruled in their favor. The pair won their freedom and received 30 shillings in damages. The decision was monumental; it was the first known case to successfully challenge the legality of slavery under the 1780 Massachusetts Constitution. Leaning on her precedent, Massachusetts would abolish the institution two years later, and be the only state in the Union to report no enslaved people on the 1790 federal census.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: After slavery, she chose the name Elizabeth Freeman.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She started getting paid for her work, bought land, and set aside an inheritance — impossible for most enslaved people and milestones that few then could achieve, whether in bondage or note. She worked for the Sedgwick family as a paid domestic servant and gained a reputation

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: as a successful midwife. Freeman was one of the few free Black people who owned property in Stockbridge. And she dictated her last will and testament, which left valuable possessions to her daughter, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Her resilience to make sure that she was free, and what she did with her life after enslavement really stands out, said Frances Jones-Sneed, emeritus professor of history at Massachusetts College of Liberal Arts in North Adams.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Still, despite the paper trail Freeman left behind, finding her descendants proved challenging.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Shepperson learned of her connection in May. Her mother, Margaret Baldwin, died last year, and a year later, the funeral director reached out to Shepperson with a strange message: A researcher was trying to contact her about her family history.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Reluctantly, she called Lindsay Fulton, chief research officer

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: of the genealogy organization American Ancestors.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Skeptical, Shepperson recalled telling Fulton: "Tell me more than something that can be found in vital statistics, or we can end the call."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Before the conversation, 10 Million Names brainstormed a list of famous enslaved people whose descendants researchers would like to find. Inspired by the 2022 unveiling of an Elizabeth Freeman statue in Sheffield, Field, of Tufts, and her colleague Kerri Greenidge, an associate professor in race, colonialism, and diaspora studies at Tufts, suggested Freeman.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Fulton and two genealogists spent months tracing Freeman's family tree, poring over the documents she left behind, specifically her will, which listed her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren by name.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: They requested birth certificates,marrige licenses, and death records. They sifted

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: through newspaper archives and Civil War pensions. They followed the family's lineage across state lines and into Connecticut, where they found a name: Margaret Baldwin,a woman seven generations away from Freeman.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But they got stuck Until Shepperson,Baldwin's daughter,returned Fulton's messengers.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I don't know what happened here, but for whatever reason, Lisa had enough faith to call me," Fulton said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Shepperson's knowledge of her family history is limited. Her mother was born in New Haven County, Conn., and was abandoned by her birth mother from an early age. Her maternal grandfather, Freeman's direct descendant, wasn't present in her mom's childhood, either, Shepperson said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Shepperson's mother and grandparents didn't reunite until later in her mother's life. But years that could've been spent learning where she came from, and repairing broken relationships, were already gone.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The family story "got lost in the shuffle around of people," Shepperson said. "Nobody sat down to talk about it."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: So when Field and Greidge revealed her ancestral connection during a Zoom call, Shepperson "didn't even have the words." Her voice cracked with emotion. If only her mother or grandmother knew the power they came from, she said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It's the strength my mom needed," she said. "The strength my grandmother, who gave all her kids up, didn't have."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: It's been a few months since Shipperson learned of her connection to Freeman. While she doesn't yet know everything about her family's history, she hopes her visit to Western Mastans will ensure future generations have the knowledge within reach.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: On Monday morning, Shepperson stepped out of a black sedan and onto the green pasture that researchers determined  was then once Freeman's property.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: It was moving to see what Freeman had come to own, but

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: learning about her life left Shepperson with more questions, too: How had her ancestors lost the modest parcel she stood upon? Why was the centuries-old tombstone unkept for so many years? Were the land, jewelry, and clothing Freeman bequeathed to her loved ones ever received?

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But with time and intensive research, Shepperson hopes she can find some answers soon.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: There is one quote in particular from Freeman that has given Shepperson newfound strength. She learned of it through a biography by Catharine Sedgwick, an author and daughter of Theodora Sedgwick, whom Freeman cared for while working for the family.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Any time while I was a slave, if one minute's freedom had been offered to me, and I had been told that I must die at the end of that minute, I would have taken it just to stand one minute on God's earth a free woman," Sedgwick wrote Freeman saying.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Shepperson taped a copy of the quote on her work computer.

layout_dets.label: 段落

layout_dets.label: 段落

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: As a July 15 deadline looms for bids to buy Steward Health Care's eight Massachusetts hospitals out of bankruptcy, months of quiet talks have intensified into what insiders describe as a high-stakes game of chicken between the Healey administration and the hospitals' landlords.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: State officials and their allies on Capitol Hill are pressing Medical Properties Trust and Macquarie Infrastructure Partners - which together own the real estate Steward occupies - to either sell the properties or lease out long-term leases that currently oblige the eight hospitals to pay more than $100 million a year.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The concessions would make buying and running the hospitals more financially feasible for new owners,according to several parties briefed on the talks.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: They spoke on the condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to discuss private negotiations.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: MPT and Macquarie, they said, have so far resisted calls to revamp the leases and may be waiting for a state commitment - which has yet to come - to provide financial backing to new hospital owners. Hanging in the public eye is the fate of the hospitals and the shape of the health care market in Eastern Massachusetts.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ed Markey weighed in Tuesday with a letter to the property owners backing the state's position and urging a "long-term reduction in lease payments, early termination of leases, or other measures that new operators can be found to keep Steward's Massachusetts hospitals open and viable."
