layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: With ERs overwhelmed, patients will be diverted to urgent cares

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: By Jason Laughlin

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: GLOBE STAFF

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Faced with crushing numbers of patients at hospitals in Eastern Massachusetts, the state Department of Public Health launched an initiative Wednesday to improve the overwhelmed emergency departments by diverting patients to urgent care centers.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Through the end of September, the state's health insurers will cover treatment at urgent care centers even if the facility is outside their coverage network, according to a DPH memo. Urgent care providers, who treat patients with non-life-threatening conditions, also agreed not to bill patients for the remaining balance after insurance reimbursement.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "What the DPH has done is unprecedented,”said Jim Brennan, president of the Massachusetts Urgent Care Association, an industry group. The Department of Health is preemptively trying to make sure all patients are aware of resources they have above and beyond the

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: emergency room."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The move comes amid extraordinary strain on the region's hospitals, with summer also the busiest time for ERs. Meanwhile, providers are still reeling from pandemic-era workforce shortages and, this year, must also contend with difficulties at Steward Health Care, the largest for-profit hospital system in the country, which operates seven active hospitals in Massachusetts. Steward declared bankruptcy in May and has curtailed some services.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It's an already strained emergency department ecosystem in Massachusetts," said Michael Caljouw, vice president of government and regulatory affairs for Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts, the state's largest private insurer. "Looking forward, we want to make sure we're all prepared for contingency care demands during the summertime if and when Steward changes occur."

layout_dets.text: Arizona abortion-rights supporters delivered signatures to the capitol Wednesday to get a measure on the November ballot.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Groups say more signatures than needed turned in

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
By Walter Berry and Anita Snow
ASSOCIATED PRESS

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: PHOENIX — Organizers in Arizona and Nebraska said Wednesday that they turned in far more signatures than required to get ballot measures on abortion rights before voters in November's election.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In Nebraska, there could be two competing questions. One, like the Arizona proposal, would add a right to abortion to the state constitution. The other would enshrine Nebraska's current ban on most abortions after 12 weeks of pregnancy.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In both states, it's now up to election officials to certify the signatures before they're added to ballots.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Democrats have made abortion rights a central message since the US Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022 and it is a key part of their efforts in this year's elections. Activists in Arkansas are still pushing to meet Friday's deadline to make the ballot there.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In five other states, the issue already is set to go before voters this year: Colorado, Florida, Maryland, Nevada, and South Dakota. The state has a measure that advocates say would protect abortion access.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Arizona organizers say they submitted 823,685 signatures, far above the 383,923 required from registered voters. County election officials have until Aug. 22 to verify whether enough of the 100,000 signatures will and provide results to the Arizona secretary of state's office.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Arizona currently has a 15- week abortion ban . The pro

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: posed amendment would allow abortions until a fetus could survive outside the womb, typically around 24 weeks, with exceptions to save the mother's life or to protect her physical or mental health. It would restrict the state from adopting or enforcing any law that would prohibit access to the procedure.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Opponents say it goes too far

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: and could lead to unlimited and unregulated abortions in Arizona. Supporters say a change in the state's constitution is necessary to ensure abortion rights cannot be easily erased by a court decision or legislative vote.

layout_dets.label: 段落

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: of Arizona and Planned Parenthood of Arizona, turned in 300 boxes of signed petitions to the secretary of state's office, where extra security has been added.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Arizona for Abortion Access spokesperson Dawn Penich said it was the most signatures ever submitted for a citizens initiative in state history.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: That was our goal from the

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: get-go,” Penich said. “We started collecting signatures in September and October 2023 and saw how passionate people are about this issue.”

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In April, the Arizona Supreme Court upheld a 1864 abortion ban that permitted abortions only to save the mother's life and provided no exceptions for survivors of rape or incest, but the Republican-controlled Legislature voted for a repeal of the Civil War-era ban, and Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs quickly signed. The 19th Amendment to the Supreme Court blocked since the US Supreme Court's decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization that eliminated constitutional protections for abortion.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The current 15-week ban was signed into law in 2022 and includes exceptions in cases of medical emergencies and has restrictions on medication abortion. It also requires an ultrasound examination, an abortion is done, as well as parental consent for minors.

layout_dets.text: In Nebraska, officials with Protect Our Rights said they turned in 207,000 signatures in their effort to enshrine abortion rights. Organizers of SBA ProLife America's competing petition effort said they submitted more than 205,000 signatures.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Justice Dept. plans to pursue Trump cases past Election Day

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
By Devlin Barrett and Perry Stein
WASHINGTON POST

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Justice Department officials plan to pursue the criminal cases against Donald Trump past Election Day even if he wins, under the belief that department rules against charging or prosecuting a sitting federal attorney will break in until Inauguration Day in January, according to people familiar with the discussions.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: That approach may become more consequential given this week’s Supreme Court ruling on presidential immunity, which probably will lead to further delays to Trump’s election interference trial in Washington, D.C., and has already affected one of his state cases.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Senior law enforcement officials have long viewed the two federal indictments against Trump - the 45th president and the presumptive Republican nominee in this year's election - as operating with potential time constraints. That's because of longstanding Justice Department policy that officials cannot criminally charge a sitting president.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Lawyers in the department do not believe the policy bars them from proceeding against a president-elect, however, according to the people familiar with the discussions, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal deliberations.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The plan to continue filing motions, seeking court hearings, and potentially conducting a trial between Election Day and Inauguration Day underscores the highly unusual nature of prosecuting not just a former president, but also possibly a future one. In the

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: months after winning election, a president-elect assumes some of the trappings of the office, such as more security and high-level briefings, but that is not the commander in chief.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In the midst of a presidential election in which criminal cases have played a central role, any court activity involving a president-elect would push American politics deeper into uncharted territory. Ultimately, the courts will be able to decide when and how to hold hearings or a trial involving a president-elect.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "The Justice Department isn't governed by the election calendar. Its prosecution of Trump is based on the law, the facts and the Justice Manual - the department's bible that lays out the post-Watergate norms that have prevented it from being weaponized," said Anthony Coley, a former Justice Department spokesman for Attorney General Merrick Garland who left the agency last year. "Until those norms change, or they're ordered otherwise, I'd expect this Justice Department to be full speed ahead. And they should be."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Current officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity, expressed the same sentiment - that if Trump wins the election, the clock on the two federal cases against him would be 10pm Jan.20, when he would be sworn in as the 47th president.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A spokesman for special counsel Jack Smith declined to comment.Trump spokesman Steven Cheung said the criminal cases against Trump are"hoaxes"that“are imploding as their collective efforts to interfere in the election have mas sively backfired."

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Israel pushes ahead with West Bank land taking

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Move sparks global censure, threatens safety

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
By Julia Frankel  
ASSOCIATED PRESS

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: JERUSALEM — Israel has approved the largest seizure of land in the occupied West Bank in over three decades, a settlement tracking group said Wednesday, a move that is likely to worsen already soaring tensions linked to the war in Gaza.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Israel's aggressive expansion in the West Bank reflects the settler community's strong influence in the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the most religious and nationalist in the country's history. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, a settler himself, has turbocharged the policy of expansion, seizing new authorities over settlement development and saying he aims to solidify Israel's hold on the territory and prevent the creation of a Palestinian state.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Authorities recently approved the appropriation of 12.7 square kilometers (nearly 5 square miles) of land in the Jordan Valley, according to a copy of the order obtained by the Associated Press. Data from Peace Now, the tracking group,indi

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: cate it was the largest single appropriation approved since the 1993 Oslo Accords at the start of the peace process.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Settlement monitors said the land grab connects Israeli settlements along a key corridor bordering Jordan, a move they said undermines the prospect of a contiguous Palestinian state.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: UN spokesperson Stephanie Dujarric called it "a step in the wrong direction," adding that "the direction we want to be heading is to find a negotiated two-state solution."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The newly seized land is in an area of the West Bank where, even before the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas war, settler violence was displacing communities of Palestinians. That violence has only surged since Hamas's Oct. 7 attack ignited the war in Gaza. Settlers have carried out more than 1,000 attacks on Palestinians since October in the West Bank, causing deaths and damaging property, according to the UN.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The land seizure, which was approved late last month but only publicized on Wednesday, comes after the seizure of 8 square kilometers (roughly 3 square miles) of land in the center of the March and 2.6 square kilometers (1 square mile in February).

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: That makes 2024 by far the

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: peak year for Israeli land seizure in the West Bank, Peucey said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: By declaring them state lands, the government opens them up to being leased to Israelis and prohibits private Palestinian ownership. This year's land seizures are contiguous, linking two already existing settlements to create a solid block of territory, the border with Jordan. The lands were declared to be closed military zones before they were declared state land.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Palestinians view the expansion of settlements in the occupied West Bank as the main barrier to any lasting peace agreement, preventing any possibility of a cohesive state. Most of the national community considers settlements illegal or illegitimate.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Israel captured the West Bank, the Gaza Strip, and east Jerusalem in the 1967 Mideast war, territories the Palestinians want for a future state. Israel's current government considers the West Bank to be the historical and religious heartland of the Jewish people and opposes Palestinian statehood.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Israel has built well over 100 settlements across the West Bank, some of which resemble fully developed suburbs or small towns. They are home to

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: ZAIN JAAFAR/AFP

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A Palestinian woman walked on the rubble of her home in the West Bank, destroyed by Israeli strikes.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: over 500,000 Jewish settlers who have Israeli citizenship.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The 3 million Palestinians in the West Bank live under seemingly open-ended Israeli military rule. The Palestinian Authority administers enclaves scattered across the territory, but is barred from operating in 60 percent of the West Bank,which includes the settlements as well as areas with a population of hundreds of thousands of Palestinians.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Yoni Mizrachi, the head of settlement tracking at Peace Now, described the land grab announced Wednesday as part of a strategy to establish a buffer zone between Jordan and Pales

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: tinian lands and choke off the practical possibility of a Palestinian state. The aim, he believes, is to push Palestinians into isolated islands surrounded by Israeli land.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "They definitely see this area as a strategic area, as the first and one of the easiest ways to begin annexation," he said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Prominent human rights organizations have pointed to Israel's rule over the West Bank in accusing it of the international crime of apartheid, allegations that acts as an attack on its legitimacy.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Smotrich was granted expanded powers over Israel's administration of the occupied territory under Netanyahu's governing coalition. Smotrich laid out his plans for the West Bank at a conference with his ultranationalist Religious Zionism Party last month, a recording of which was obtained by Peace Now. He said he intended to appropriate up to 15 square kilometers (nearly 6 square miles) of land in the West Bank this year.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "We came to settle the land, to build it, and to prevent its division and the establishment of a Palestinian state, God forbid," he said during the conference. He vowed to "change the map back to history" by claiming more West Bank land than ever before as state land.

layout_dets.text: BEIRUT - An Israeli strike in southern Lebanon on Wednesday killed a senior Hezbollah commander as tensions beteen the two sides continue to boil, a Hezbollah official told the Associated Press.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The strike near the southern coastal city of Tyre took place as global diplomatic efforts have intensified in recent weeks to prevent escalating clashes between Hezbollah and the Israeli military from spiraling into an all-out war that could possibly lead to a direct confrontation between Israel and Iran.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A Hezbollah statement identified the killed commander as Mohammad Naameh Nasser, who went by the name "Abu Naameh," his nom de guerre. A Hezbollah official, speaking anonymously in line with reguements, said he was head of the group's Aziz Unit, one of three regional divisions in southern Lebanon.

layout_dets.text: Nasser is the most senior official from the Iran-backed

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: group killed since Taleb Sami Abdullah, who was killed in an airstrike June 11. Hezballah leader Hassan Nasrallah, in a speech honoring Abdullah, said he played a pivotal role on the front line since clashes began on Oct. 8, leading the Nasr Unit

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Hezbollah said in response to the killing of Nasser, it launched Falaq rockets with heavy warheads targeting the headquarters of the Israeli military's 769th Brigade in Kiryat Shmona, as well as 100 salvo of rockets targeting the headquarters of Israel's 210th division and the Kilaal air base in the Israeli-occupied Syrian Golan Heights.

layout_dets.label: 段落

layout_dets.label: 段落

layout_dets.label: 段落

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Hezbollah'll"militants in southern Lebanon. It said Nasser led attacks from southwestern Lebanon.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Hezbollah launched rockets on northern Israel a day after a Hamas surprise attack on southern Israel in October, leading to limited clashes along the tense border. The attacks have since gradually escalated, with Hezbollah introducing new weapons in their attacks and Israel striking deeper into Lebanon.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The group maintains that it will stop its attacks once there is

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: a cease-fire in the Gaza Strip. Until then, it says it will continue with its attacks to pile pressure on Israel and the international community. Israeli officials have threatened to launch counter military operations, but should Hezbollah not stop its attacks.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Hezbollah deputy leader Sheikh Naim Kassem said in an interview Monday that Israel cannot expect the group's attacks to remain limited should it launch a military operation within Lebanon,even if it aims.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: to keep the conflict below the threshold of all-out war. Allies, including thousands of Iran-backedilitamen in Iraq, have offered to join Hezbollah on the front lines.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Israeli airstrikes on Lebanon since October have killed over 450 people, most of them Hezbollah fighters, but the dead also include more than 80 civilians and noncombatants. On the Israeli side, 16 soldiers and 11 civilians have been killed in a massacre by Gaza begun. Tens of thousands of people on both sides of the tense frontier have been displaced in the monthslong war.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Senior adviser to President Biden, Amos Hochstein, who has been shuttling between Lebanon and Israel, is set to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron's Lebanon envoy Jean-Yves Le Daniel in Paris on Wednesday as part of his ongoing diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.

layout_dets.label: 段落

layout_dets.text: FREETOWN, Sierra Leone - A bill that bans child marriage in Sierra Leone has been signed into law, President Julius Maada Bio said late Tuesday, in an effort to protect girls in the West African region where about a third are married before adulthood.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The law is being celebrated widely. It criminalizes marrying any girl who is under 18 years old. Offenders face up to 15 years in prison or a fine of around \(4,000 or both. Witnesses to such marriages will also face jail or a fine.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I have always believed that the future of Sierra Leone is female," Bio said on social media platform X. "This and future generations of girls must thrive in Sierra Leone in which they're protected, equal, and empowered."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Sierra Leone is home to 800,000 child brides, with half of them married before age 15, according to the UNs children's agency.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: First Lady Fatima Bio was among the key champions of the law, which also provides improved access to education and support services for children affected by child marriage.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: TAIPEI, Taiwan - Taiwan said Wednesday that China warned its coast guard against interfering in the detention of a Taiwanese fishing boat, in what was seen as Beijing's latest attempt to assert its territorial claims in the Taiwan Strait.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The incident comes as tensions have risen following Taiwan's election of President William Lai Ching-te, whose party rejects unification with the mainland, and a threat by Beijing to execute supporters of Taiwanese independence.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Liu Dejun, a spokesperson for China's coast guard, said Wednesday that the Taiwanese fishing boat was detained on suspicion of illegal fishing. Liu said the boat violated a fishing moratorium in Chinese waters by allowing the captain to swim in one zone. Liu said the boat also was using nets that were finer than allowed by Chinese law.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Taiwan's coast guard repeated its call for there lease of the boat and its crew members,who were taken from waters off the Taiwanese controlled island of Kinmen just off the Chinese coast on Tuesday night.

layout_dets.text: KINGSTON, Jamaica — Hurricane Beryl was roaring by Jamaica on Wednesday, with islanders scrambling to make preparations after the powerful Category 5 storm earlier killed by a boat and caused significant damage in the southeast Caribbean.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In Kingston, people boarded up windows, fishermen pulled their boats out of the water, and workers dismantled roadside advertising boards to protect them from the lashing winds.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A hurricane warning was in effect for Jamaica, Grand Cayman, Little Cayman, and Cayman Brac. Beryl was forecast to weaken slightly over the next day or two, but still be at or near major-hurricane strength when it passes near or over Jamaica. The Cayman Islands on Thursday and into Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula on Friday, according to the US National Hurricane Center.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Jamaica was under a state of emergency as the island was declared a disaster zone hours before the impact of Hurricane Beryl.

layout_dets.label: 段落

It is unclear how closely Obama addressed Biden's performance and his path to reelection on the call.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: President Biden is grateful for President Obama's unwavering support since the very start of this campaign as both a powerful messenger to voters and a trusted adviser directly to the president, Lauren Hitt, a special assistant to Biden campaign, said in a statement. A spokesperson for Obama declined to comment.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Obama has long harbored worries about his party defeating Donald Trump in November, which is expected to be a recent month about how chal

layout_dets.label: 段落

layout_dets.label: 段落

He sees his role as being helpful to Biden based on their history of working together, the people said. On Friday, Obama appeared at a fundraiser in New York for House Democrats, where he expressed continued support for Biden.

layout_dets.label: 段落

But this election is still a choice between someone who has fought for ordinary folks his entire life and someone who only cares about himself. Between someone who tells the truth; who knows right from wrong and will give it to the American people is true and someone lives through his teeth for his own benefit. Last night didn't change that, and it's why so much is at stake in November."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But for months, Obama has

layout_dets.label: 段落

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: MSNBC hosts have harsh words on president

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Over the past \(31\%\) years, liberal hosts on MSNBC reliably provided support for President Biden and trained fire on his adversaries, notably Donald Trump.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But in the days since Biden's halting debate performance, there has been a different reality on the network that employs two of his former top aides. Some have issued harsh reviews; some have even raised questions about his campaign and fitness for office.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It was not a good performance," Symone Sanders-Townsend, a former Biden White House senior adviser turned MSNBC host and pundits, said Tuesday morning. She added that "the chatter will not end" about Biden's age.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "No one who watched with their eyes thought that was a good performance," said Jen

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Psaki, Biden's former press secretary, who also hosts a show on the network.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The new dynamic started immediately after Thursday's debate when a panel of MSNBC luminaries took an even harder edge.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden's job was to calm his party, said MSNBC host Joy Reid. "To make them feel that: 'Yes, I can do this. I have four more years in me. I have the ability and the strength to do four more years.' He did not do that. He did the opposite of that."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Media observers took note of MSNBC's tone, considering the network's longtime role as a balm for the anxiety of its left-leaning viewers.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It was remarkable what those guys said," said one veteran cable news anchor, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to talk candidly.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "We knew what Fox was going to say, and I had a pretty good idea of what CNN was going to say, but the question was what MSNBC going to say, because that's really where a lot of the messaging and alignment with the Democratic Party comes from," said Democratic strategist Michael Starr Hopkins. "And for MSNBC hosts to come out and say, 'Wow, this guy can't do it,' that was really telling."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Perhaps the most significant shift occurred on the network's morning show "Morning Joe," which has reliably trumpeted Biden and hosted relatively sympathetic interviews with the president and Vice President Kamala Harris.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden is known to be a power-watcher of the morning show and reportedly speaks regularly with co-host Joe Scarborough. That's what made it so surprising when the host began his Friday morning broadcast by saying that Biden "tragically did not rise to the occasion last night."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Scarborough said he loves the president and believes he has had a productive administration. But, he added, "Donald Trump lied over and over and over and over again, and Joe Biden couldn't respond to any of those lies."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Most strikingly, Scarborough predicted that Trump would win reelection in November "unless things change."

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: US allies see a worrisome turn in presidential immunity ruling

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Several partners have nothing like these protections

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
By Motoko Rich  
NEW YORK TIMES

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: TOKYO - Allies of the United States had already been looking at the country's upcoming election with anxiety. Now, with the US Supreme Court granting an unprecedented expansion of executive power by giving presidents legal immunity, analysts in some of those countries are even more concerned about the reliability of American power.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Across Asia and Europe, where allied leaders have grown accustomed to dealing with threats from authoritarian leaders in Russia, North Korea, and China, the idea that they might be more likely to deal with an unsettled US president is an unsettling prospect.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "If the US president is free from the restrictions of criminal law, if he has that level of criminal immunity, the other leaders of the allied nations cannot trust the US," said Keigo Komamura, a professor of law at Keio University in Tokyo. "We cannot maintain a stable national security relationship."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Komamura added that the Supreme Court's decision now gave the perception of an American president who can operate above the law. "This may be rude to the US, but it is not that different from Xi Jinping in China," he said. "The rule of law has become the rule of power."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Although some give limited immunity to leaders while in office, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and Great Britain - among the United States' closest allies in the world - offer nothing like the sweeping protec-

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: tions the Supreme Court appears to have granted in its ruling this week.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The court's decision to give the president immunity from criminal prosecution for official conduct - which was itself vaguely defined by the court - was "out of line with global norms," said Rosalind Dixon, a professor of law at the University of New South Wales in Sydney. "I think that what is occurring in the United States in terms of the court's ruling and the presidential election should be of grave concern to all of America's allies."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In South Korea, political leaders essentially have no legal protections from criminal prosecution once they are out of office and the president is limited to a single term. Four of the past eight former presidents have been convicted and imprisoned after leaving office for corruption and other crimes they committed before and while they were in office.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I think many Koreans are proud of the fact that no one is above the law, even the president," said Ramon Pacheco Pardo, a professor of international relations at King's College London and chair of Korea studies at the Brussels University. "Performance at Vrije Universiteit." But in the US, it appears that presidents are created differently from the rest of the people.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Still, the frequency of criminal indictments of officials in South Korea has contributed to increasing political polarization, with some supporting the punishments as acts of justice and others viewing them as little more than politicial revenge orchestrated by a new president.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In Japan, the constitution grants all members of Parlia

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: ment immunity from arrest while in office, but not from criminal prosecution, Komunaru said. The prime minister, who must be a member of Parliament, is covered under this clause.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: One of the biggest scandals of the 1970s in Japan was when former prime minister Kakuei Tanaka was indicted on bribery charges for having accepted $1.6 million from Lockheed to arrange the purchase of aircraft by All Nippon Airways, Japan's largest airline.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Even in countries where there is some immunity for political leaders, it is usually more narrowly defined. In Britain, where members of Parliament broadly enjoy legal protections from prosecution for political speech, they are not immune from the criminal laws that govern the public.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The police fined former prime minister Boris Johnson, for example, while he was still in office for attending a lockdown party at Downing Street that broke coronavirus laws that his own Cabinet had instituted during the pandemic.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Even where legal immunity is more strictly defined, though, the laws may not be as big a factor as political culture.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In Malaysia, although executive immunity is not as sweeping as the US Supreme Court just granted to presidents, a culture of impunity has meant that few leaders are taken to court despite widespread corruption.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In Israel, all members of Parliament, including the prime minister, are subject to absolute immunity from prosecution of acts committed while performing their initial duties. It is a protection not unlike that defined by the US Supreme Court ruling.

layout_dets.text: Call 2nd Trump term a threat to democracy

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
By Kenneth P. Vogel  
NEW YORK TIMES

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A group of business leaders is calling on President Biden to step aside and make way for a replacement atop the Democratic Party's presidential ticket.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Leadership Now Project, a coalition of 400 politically active current and retired executives who mostly but not entirely lean left, issued a statement on Wednesday urging Biden to “pass the torch of this year’s

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: presidential nomination to the next generation of highly capable Democrats.”

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The statement is unsigned, but Daniella Ballou-Aares, the group's founder and CEO, said that it was supported by an overwhelming majority of the 100 leaders of Leadership Now Project.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The membership includes Jeni Britton Bauer, founder of Jeni's Famous Ice Cream; Thomas W. Florsheim Jr., CEO of the footwear maker Wayco Group; Eddie Fishman, managing director of the investment firm D.E. Shaw & Co.; John Pepper, former CEO of Procter & Gamble; and Paul Tagliabue,

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: former commissioner of the NFL.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The statement comes as major Democratic donors are increasingly concluding that the

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: 'This sense that [Biden's decision] is a small group family decision is not good for democracy.'

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: DANIELLA BALLOU-AARES, CEO, Leadership Now Project

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: party would stand a better chance of holding the White House with a different nominee in the wake of Biden's weak performance in last week's presi

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: dential debate with Donald Trump. But most donors and big money groups on the left have refrained from going public out of concern about generat

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: ing a backlash.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In its statement, Leadership Now Project called the prospect of a second Trump term "an existential threat to American de

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: mocracy” and said that at the debate Biden “failed to effectively make the case against Trump, and we now fear the risk of a devastating loss in November.”

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The statement added that "we have heard from many individuals who share our deep concerns about the present course but fear speaking out" and concluded by imploring others "to join us in making this urgent call."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In an interview, BallouAares, a business executive who was a senior State Department adviser during the Obama administration, said he had been disturbed by the messaging from the White House and other

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: er Biden supporters in recent days.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "This sense that this is a small group family decision is not good for democracy," she said, calling it "really inconsistent with where people were after watching the debate."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Her group, which consists of nonprofit arms and a political action committee, has endorsed candidates from both parties, and recently hosted at its annual meeting former Representative Adam Kinzinger, an anti- Trump Republican, and Governor Gretchen Whitmer of Michigan, a Democrat mentioned as a possible replacement for Biden.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Biden well aware of stakes heading into weekend, allies say

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: BIDEN

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Continued from Page A1

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: knowledge that his next few appearances heading into the July 4 holiday weekend must go well, particularly an interview scheduled for Friday with George Stephanopoulos of ABC News and campaign stops in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "He knows if he has two more events like that, we're in a different place" by the end of the weekend, said one of the allies, referring to Biden's halting and unfocused performance in the debate. That person, who talked to his president in the past 24 hours, spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive situation.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The accounts of his conversations with allies are the first indication to become public that the president is seriously considering whether he can recover after a devastating performance on the debate stage in Atlanta last Thursday.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A new poll from The New York Times and Siena College showed that former President Donald Trump now leads Biden 49 percent to 43 percent among likely voters nationally, a 3-point swing toward the Republican from just a week earlier, before the debate. The 6-point deficit underscored the growing challenges to the campaign and could make it harder to hang on.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Karine Jean-Pierre, the White House press secretary, said the president told her directly that he had not talked to allies about dropping out of the race.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "That is absolutely false," she said during the briefing. While batting down speculation about Biden stepping down, Jean-Pierre also referred to Harris, who is seeing a surge of support among Democrats, as "the future of the party."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: One of Biden's allies, a top adviser to him, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the president was "well aware of the political challenge he faces."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: That person said Biden was aware that the outcome of his campaign could be different from what he is fighting for. Biden, that person said, believes he is an effective leader who is mentally sharp and "doesn't get how others don't accept that."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Times reported Tuesday that several current and former officials and others who encountered the president behind closed doors noticed that he increasingly appeared confused or listless, or would lose the thread of conversations, in the weeks and months before the debate.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden still adamantly views his debate showing as a bad performance, the person said, not a revelatory event about his capacity to do the job for four more years.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Key party donors have been privately calling House members, senators, super PACs, the Biden campaign, and the White House to say that they think Biden should step down, according to Democrats familiar with the discussion.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: On Wednesday, Reed Hastings, the Netflix cofounder who in recent years has become one of the biggest donors to the Democratic Party, called on Biden to relinquish his place at the top of the ticket.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Biden needs to step aside to allow a vigorous Democratic leader to beat Trump and keep us safe and prosperous," he said in an email to the Times.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: An elected Democrat, speaking on the condition of anonymity given the political sensitivities, said the decision is still ultimately up to Biden. "The only thing that matters is his decision on whether or not he's going to let it go," that person said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Inside the White House, senior officials tried to calm nerves in a staff-wide conference call. Jeff Zients, the White House chief of staff, told members of the president's staff that they should keep their heads down and "execute, execute, execute."

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: JIM WATSON/AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: President Biden arrived to speak at a Medal of Honor ceremony in the East Room of the White House on Wednesday.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Zients also told them to "hold their heads up" and be proud, a contradiction that he admitted had an element of humor to it.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Later in the day, Zients appeared on a separate call, a weekly check-in among Biden's Cabinet officials, and echoed much of the talking points he shared with staff members, according to a person familiar with the call.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden had been slow to personally reach out to key Democrats to assuage their concerns, which had fueled anger in the party and frustrated some of his own advisers. According to Jean-Pierre, the president has now "connected with" Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader in the House; Senator Chuck Schumer of New Jersey, the Democratic leader; Representative Nancy Pelosi of California, the former speaker; Representative James E. Clyburn of South Carolina; and Senator Chris Coons of Delaware.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The president had lunch with Harris at the White House and

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: later the pair met with Democratic governors. Until now, Biden has focused on speaking with trusted advisers and family members, who have urged him to stay in the race.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "The president shared he is staying in the race," texted Governor Josh Green of Hawaii, who attended the meeting with governors virtually. "He shared candidly he was exhausted the day of the debate, and was very direct about that. The president was clear and focused in our meeting, and I found him to be solid . . . I suspect people will need to see the president in person and on TV to be convinced he is up to it. He is."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: An aide to Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey declined to comment on the meeting.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Representative Debbie Dingell, Democrat of Michigan, said during an interview on MSNBC that Biden still must do more to address the public.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "He's got to show the Ameri

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: can people that he can do this job," she said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Key donors expressed exasperation that he did not join a campaign call Monday meant to assuage them. And some Democrats have grown increasingly suspicious that the president'steam has not been fully forthcoming about the impact that aging has had on him.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Democratic leaders in the House and Senate were not urging their members to rally around Biden on Wednesday. Instead, they were listening to myriad complaints about the president's handling of the situation from across the party.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Several allies of Biden have underscored that he is still in the fight of his political life and that he largely sees this moment as a chance to come back from being counted out, as he has done many times throughout his half-century career. At the same time, they said, he is clear-eyed about how uphill the battle will be.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden's team had sought to

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: build a firewall by persuading elected Democrats and well-known party figures not to publicly call on him to drop out. But Representative Lloyd Doggett of Texas became the first Democratic member of Congress to say on Tuesday that the president should step aside. Two others – representatives of the U.S. and Marie Ghesuenkamp Perez of Washington – said they believed he would lose in November.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In a statement Wednesday, Representative Seth Moulton, Democrat of Massachusetts, cast doubt over Biden's chances in November.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Winning will require prosecuting the case in the media, in town halls, and at campaign stops all over the country," he said. "President Biden needs to demonstrate that he can do that. The unfortunate reality is that the status quo will likely deliver us President Trump."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Others have indicated privately that they may follow suit and speak out.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Say president can't withdraw from campaign

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
By Isaac Arnsdorf, Josh Dawsey, and Marianne Levine  
WASHINGTON POST

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Donald Trump and his campaign hope President Biden stays in the race, according to four people familiar with private discussions, believing they can beat him even with Trump's felony conviction and other charges. But they are also ramping up attacks on Vice President Kamala Harris.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Publicly, Trump and his allies have dismissed suggestions that Biden could withdraw from the race, insisting that it is too late for Democrats to change course. Privately, they have started preparing for different possibilities, that even it could be harder to beat another Democrat who is not Biden or Harris.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I'm going to show up and I'm going to campaign whether it's him or somebody else."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Trump said in a Monday interview with Richmond, Va., radio host John Reid, referencing polls showing him doing as well or better against other Democrats.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "The funny thing is we're beating him badly in the polls, but nobody else is doing any better," he added in an interview that aired Monday with radio host John Fredericks.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Letting Biden be the focus of attention is unusual for Trump, who is more accustomed to dominating the headlines. But he has laid low since the debate, with no public events scheduled. A running mate candidate was elected as early as next week, with the Republican National Convention to follow the week after.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Trump campaign's message to surrogates after last week's debate was that Biden is the Democratic nominee, and Democrats are stuck with him, according to a Republican close to the campaign, who like others interviewed for this story, wasn't authorized to speak publicly. Biden struggled through the 90-minute faceoff, setting

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: off widespread alarm in his party.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It sure seems they want Biden to stay on the ticket. They think he's vulnerable, and they like where they're at. You can see they are not excited at all about the prospect of him leaving," said David Axelrod, a longtime top strategist to Barack Obama.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Trump advisers were pri

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: vately stunned at how poorly Biden performed, people familiar with the matter said, believing he would be a stronger debater.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Taylor Budowich, who leads Trump's outside PAC, said the clips from Thursday's debate "would make for devastating campaign commercials." But Budowich also said that Harris being the nominee "has the ad

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: team tackling with excitement. On Wednesday the PAC, known as MAGA Inc., circulated an attack on Harris, headlined, "Is Invasion Czar Kamala Harris The Best They Got?"

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden's campaign and the White House have insisted the president remains committed to running and are planning a fresh bout of campaign events and at least one television interview. The campaign announced raising $127 million in June, ending the month with $240 million cash on hand, compared to Trump's $111.8 million raised and $285 million in the bank.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The incumbent and his aides have sought to stay on the attack against Trump, hitting him over abortion and the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol by a pro-Trump mob, among other issues. On Monday, Biden responded to a Supreme Court decision on presidential immunization, saying it would leave Trump "more emboldened to do whatever he pleases" in a second term.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Trump campaign expects he will be the Democratic

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: nominee, Trump spokeswoman Karoline Leavitt said. "We are confident no matter what that we will be victorious in tying any Democrat on the ballot to Biden and to the Democratic Party," she added.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Trump campaign has begun airing ads suggesting Harris was celebrating Biden's struggles, showing her laughing in a way that is meant to appear villainous and collapsing the Biden-Harris campaign logo to remove the president's name. The Trump campaign is also attacking other Democratic candidates for their past defences of Biden, accusing them of covering up the president's decline.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Republicans have indicated that they would attack any Democratic effort to replace Biden as an affront to Democratic primary voters and the democratic process.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Outside the campaign, lawyers at the right-wing Heritage Foundation researched ballot access laws in all 50 states to be prepared to oppose any effort to remove or replace Biden after he officially becomes the Democratic nominee.

layout_dets.text: Healey's message to migrants: No room left

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: PAT GREENHOUSE/GLOBE STAFF

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: JOHN TLUMACKI/GLOBE STAFF/POOL/FIL

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: $\blacktriangleright$MIGRANTS

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Continued from Page AI

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: it is also offering to pay for their airline tickets through the state's "Reticting Program" to cover travel expenses for families who have a safe, long-term place to stay outside of Massachusetts. Last month, several Healey administration officials trekked to the US-Mexico border to "educate" officials and migrant families about "the lack of shelter availability in Massachusetts." The governor herself praised President Biden's order in June shutting the southern border to some asylum seekers.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I think we've been clear from the outset that Massachusetts, while we have a right-to-shelter-set, we've only had so much capacity," Healey said at an unrelated event Tuesday.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Taken together, the actions mark the starkest departure from the state's tradition of housing homeless families under the 1986 right-to-shelter law.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: It's a moment that reveals that a family's right to shelter in Massachusetts is not a limitless promise, nor is it immune to political pressures and economic realities.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: And it's a reminder that laws can't always withstand the pressure of a strained budget or a political landscape in which immigration remains a top issue of voter concern, even in liberal-leaning Massachusetts, now that a once-distant border crisis unfolds in residents' own communities.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: For more than a year, the Healey administration has, like Democratic-led states around the country, attempted to walk a fine line between upholding longstanding liberal values and managing a bona fide crisis straining state and local resources. The Obama Biden's most high-profile surrogates while navigating an issue that has only grown more fraught since she took office in 2023.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Healey was explicit that her decision to send a team to the border was intended to send a message: "Do not come to Massachusetts if you expect housing. You can only come here if you are in the United States because we are at full capacity," she said at the Tuesday event.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Last fall, Healey for the first time imposed a new limit on how many families the state's emergency shelter system, which guarantees food and shelter for homeless and migrant families or pregnant people, could accommodate. The system hit that cap of 7,500 families months ago. Nearly 700 families sit on a wait list, with many sleeping in the airport or in temporary overflow shelter sites that face restrictions of their

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: own.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: While a recent University of Massachusetts Amherst/WCVB poll shows voters don't hold Healey directly responsible for the migrant crisis, the state is still on the hook to pay for it, and that brings political pressure. Healey's office projects it will cost $915 million to run the emergency shelter system for the fiscal year that began July 1.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The program quickly ate through the roughly $700 million allocated for the fiscal year that just ended, and required a temporary infusion to keep the program afloat. The legislation that provided that financial life-

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: line also allows her administration to take \(251 million from a surplus revenue savings account to fund the shelter system through the end of June. The bill made another \)175 million available for the current fiscal year.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: National polling by Gallup found a record-high 55 percent of Americans see illegal immigration as a "critical threat" to the United States, up from 47 percent a year ago. Among Democrats, that number climbed from 20 percent in 2023 to 29 percent in 2024.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: And states are mostly hamstrung over what they can do.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Earlier this year, Healey and other governors met to urge Biden to send them money and expedite work authorization for new arrivals, but the call for help has yet to reach Congress, which represents a key step in legislative measures to address the broken immigration system.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In the meantime, Massachusetts schools are struggling, their funding eaten away by higher-than-expected inflation. Some districts say they lack the support needed to absorb migrant students, who often require translators and extra social services, though the state does give money to districts for

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In March, members of Bostonians Against Sanctuary Cities demonstrated in front of the State House. Back in January, Governor Maura Healey inspected the shelter conversion at the Melnea Cass Recreational Complex.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: each migrant student enrolled. The MBTA remains drastically underfunded even as it continues to provide unreliable service. And the perception that the state is spending too much money on outsiders has caused an uproar in some Massachusetts communities.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The crisis is exacerbated by an acute housing shortage and an unproductive Congress that's failed to help states struggling with large numbers of migrant arrivals, said Jennie Murray, president and CEO of the National Immigration Forum.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It is quite a shame," she said. "We can't solve the issue at the state level if we don't have money from Congress."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Healey isn't the only governor who has waded through choppy political waters on the issue. In 2014, President Barack Obama asked Governor Deval Patrick if Massachusetts would be willing to house several hundred million American children who had crossed the US-Mexico border, Patrick obliged, and criticism followed.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Patrick, like Healey, was

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: grounded in his belief that it was the best thing for the state, said Doug Rubin, who served as a top adviser to Patrick at the time. He said Healey has succeeded in "standing up for the values that we have in Massachusetts . . . while balancing all that during this crisis."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "You can survive vagaries of the political moment in time and people will respect you," Rubin said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Danielle Ferrier, CEO of Heading Home, said she doesn't fault Healey, who is the only governor in the country working within the confines of a right-to-shelter law. Heading Home contracts with the state to provide hundreds of family shelter units in the Boston and Lawrence arrements, as well as a yet-to-beopened shelter inside the closed Bay State Correctional Center in Norfolk.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: From Ferrier's perspective, Healey is trying to meet competing demands.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It is really hard sitting in the pressure of a new policy," she said of the new limits on shelter stays. "At the same time, there are families still waiting to come in right into the shelter system. I'm sure that people walked into an impossible situation. There is no easy solution."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Others, however, don't give Healey as much credit.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Etel Haxhiah, a longtime homeless and housing advocate and city councilor in Worcester, said the administration's recent actions "send the wrong message." Instead of limiting the number of people in shelters, he said that he would invest more resources in affordable housing and ways to transition people out of shelters.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "The right to shelter seems to be getting diluted," she said. "They might as well remove it instead of putting limits that don't really resolve the issue."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Pressed if immigrants are still welcome here, Healey said Tuesday that it is important for people outside of Massachusetts to "understand the state of play.”

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I think it's irresponsible and inhumane to let people proceed thinking that there is housing in Massachusetts available to them and their families when there is not," Healey said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Massachusetts has stepped up and done an awful lot, and I'm grateful to those who we've worked with in partnership, and grateful to communities," she added. "But I think any other course would be irresponsible."

layout_dets.label: 段落

layout_dets.text: Impending loss of airport sanctuary leaves many at a loss

layout_dets.text: Local volunteers handed out bags with toothbrushes and other supplies to families sleeping at Logan Airport.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: LOGAN

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Continued from Page A1

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: offered shelter to families as the state, with its overburdened emergency shelter system, continues to be buffeted by a migrant crisis fueled in large part by violent unrest and economic turnmoil in Latin America.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Healey's policy shift is intended to lessen the strain on state resources as the number of new arrivals continues to overwhelm the shelter system. The change follows a trip by administration members to five Texas towns near the US-Mexico border to educate border officials and migrant families about the maxed-out shelters in Massachusetts.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Healey's administration is also offering to pay for their airline tickets through the state's "Reticiting Program." The program covers travel expenses if families have a safe, long-term place to stay outside of Massachusetts.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Louissaint fled Cap-Haitien in Haiti, where she worked in restaurants and hotels and as a street vendor, to seek a better life. After living for some years in Brazil, she recently crossed into the United States at Brownsville, Texas. She arrived at Logan on Monday with three children and her partner, Larisa, who had been involved in guard and glass worker in his homeland. They had heard that in Boston, "they help people, they help families" navigate the immigration system, Louissaint said. She has no friends or fami

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: ly in the region.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "We are really sad to hear that," she said of the Logan deadline through an interpreter.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Others shared her sentiment.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Of course I'm stressed about that," said Jean Iliodor, a 43-year-old Haitian who has been staying at Terminal E with his wife and 3-year-old son since mid-June.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "We picked Boston as the best state to come to because at least we could stay in the airport until we figured it out," he said through an interpreter."Imagine  if we went to Florida—we would be out in the street."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "But now they're kicking us out," Iliodor said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Wednesday morning, a Healey administration spokesperson said the number of families at Logan has declined by half over the last week, as staff and providers work to help migrants find other options with friends or relatives, or, for eligible families, space in the former Bay State Correctional Center in Norfolk, which has been transformed into a shelter that can accommodate up to 140 families. As of Monday, there were 698 families on the wait list for shelter placements, according to the state.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In a statement last week, L. Scott Rice, the state's emergency assistance director, said the administration's decision is "in the best interest of families and travelers and staff at Logan, as the airport is not an appropriate place for people to seek shelter."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The new rule is not the first

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: to stop homeless families from sheltering in certain spaces in Massachusetts. Last summer, administrators at Boston Medical Center, which serves the neediest patients in the area, barred families from sheltering in emergency department, in some cases even sending them after-hours in Uber to Logan Airport.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: At Terminal E Tuesday night, many were aware of next week's deadline, but said they were unsure of their next step.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I don't have any plans, because I have no one," said Dioulie Figaro. 34.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She has been staying at the airport since June 29 with her husband and three small children. Like many here, she fled Haiti.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Earlier this week, a UN agen

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: cy announced that gang violence in Haiti has displaced more than 300,000 children since March. The country continues to struggle to curb killings and kidnappings.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Half of the nearly 580,000 people who have become homeless in the last four months are children.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The spike in violence began in late February after a series of attacks on key government infrastructure eventually led Prime Minister Ariel Henry to resign in April. The Associated Press recently reported that the news now control at least 80 percent of Port-au-Prince and the most roads leading in and out of it.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: For decades, homeless families have been guaranteed shelter under a 1980s-era law in

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Massachusetts, the only statewide right-to-shelter requirement in the United States. But as the housing crisis ramped up and unrest abroad sent more migrant north, the system has become overwhelmed.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In the fall, Healey capped capacity in state-run emergency shelters at 7,500 families - the first restriction on how many people the state would house in the system. And on May 1, state officials began to limit stays in state-run overflow shelters to 30 days, requiring people to reapply monthly.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Logan, meanwhile, has become a refuge. Near Terminal E's international arrivals gate on Tuesday, dozens of people settled in to sleep for the evening, spreading blankets, pillows, and slieeping bags along the floor,charging their phones, and blowing up portable mattresses.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Jean-Paul Alexis, 32, an electrician in Petit Goaves, Haiti, was there with his wife and 10-year-old child. He has no plans for shelter next week. Alexis fled Haiti in 2018 because of its instability, trying to settle first in Guanyan and then in Mexico. To hear him tell it, he didn't achieve anything in those locations. "I don't know," he'd give Boston a try." He pines for the days when he didn't have to sleep on the floor and "things were better for me."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: When Alexis left his home six years ago, the situation in Haiti was taking a turn for the worse, he said. Now the country has further deteriorated.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "If they were to tell me they were sending me back to Haiti, that would be heartbreaking," he said. "Total despair."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: At one point, a group of local mothers who have been visiting the migrants in the airport wheeled in carts filled with home-cooked meals, bags of produce, backpacks with toys and diapers for children, diapers and wipes, and donated clothing.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It feels like a game of chicken between Maura Healey and the federal government. And it's hurting real people," said Becky Hare, a field resident who was among those trying to help the migrants.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Marc D. Dominique came to Boston with his family because he thought there was infrastructure here that would help them navigate the various bureaucracies. A 27-year-old Port-Au-Prince's son, Dominique remains optimistic, despite the looming deadline.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I think they're going to find some place to put us by then," he said.
