layout_dets.text: ELECTION 2024

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Biden's base has been the Senate, which has gone eerily quiet since the debate

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: MATT MCLAIN/THE WASHINGTON POST

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: A visitor walks through the U.S. Capitol Rotunda in March. As senators return to Washington on Monday to talk in person for the first time since before the debate, the staunch support that President Biden has enjoyed from the chamber's Democrats may begin to wane.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: @PKCapitol PAUL KANE

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: President Biden has always considered the Senate his home away from home

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: and, for almost $3\frac{1}{2}$ years, that feeling has been pretty mutual.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Senate Democrats have been a bulwark of support for Biden. They have had the best access to him and his senior advisers. Biden's team has most often landed at the same negotiating position as Senate Democrats, whether it was moderating the more liberal posture of House Democrats in 2021-2022 or, after the majority flipped, using Senate Democrats as a blockade against far-right measures sent up by the House GOP.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: While many liberals pinned for a younger alternative during both the 2020 and 2024 primaries, Senate Democrats were more vocal in supporting the 81-year-old's reelection bid.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "You don't make trades. We have our nominee. He's the leader of the free world. He's the leader of our party and he's objectively good at this job," Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) said in a late January interview.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I think the president is in a very strong position," Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) said at the time.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Like more than two-thirds of the current Democratic caucus, Schatz, 51, and Ossoff, 37, never served a day with Biden during his 36 years in the Senate.They come from the Senate generation that only knows him as the 70something vice president and, now, an octogenarian president. But, like most Senate Democrats, they have been courted and tended to with great care by White House officials.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But as Biden's hold on the Democratic nomination has weakened after his poor debate performance against former president Donald Trump, Senate Democrats have grown less boisterous about the president's future.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: As of late Saturday, not a single Democratic senator had put forward a call for Trump to step aside, though many remain worried about his ability to run the country and whether he is up to the challenge of overcoming the crisis.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: That's in stark contrast to the House, where five Democrats have formally asked him to step aside and at least 10 others have raised concerns publicly about whether he should reconsider his plans.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But those same Senate Democrats have remained relatively quiet in a manner that

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: could suggest a more ominous future. Chamber members return to Washington to talk in person Monday for the first time since June 20, when the Senate has its midsummer legislative break.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Senate Majority Leader Charles E＿Schumer (D-N.Y.), known for his aggressive approach to home-state politics, has barely appeared in public since the June 27 debate.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I'm with Joe Biden," Schumer told reporters on Tuesday in Syracuse, vouching for the president's acumen.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: He has not made any television appearances or radio interviews to lend greater support for the president. His counsel has been kept to many one-on-one conversations, including a Wednesday call with Biden.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Behind the scenes, Sen. Mark R. Warner (Va.) has been talking with Senate Democrats about assembling a group to ask Biden to step aside, as The Washington Post's Leigh Ann Caldwell and Liz Goodwin first reported Friday.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Warner's aides did not deny the effort. Asked about the report

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: while campaigning in Wisconsin, Biden said "only"Warner had been discussing this matter.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: That response suggested it could be a politically psychological blow if a group of American senators publicly calls on Biden to step aside.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: When they do speak in public, Senate Democrats have tended to offer support he still needs to make a stronger case to sway voters.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The way he's really going to convince people is being out on the trail doing what Joe Biden does best. He's not the politician that is the best at giving a speech before a hundred thousands of dollars. Tim Kaine (D-V.) told reporters in Virginia Beach on Friday

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But Kaine, the vicepresidential nominee in 2016, left open the possibility for someone else to lead the ticket.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "If Joe Biden says, “I can do this,’ then I believe him, because he’s a man of his word and I have to believe him,’ Kaine said. ‘And if Joe Biden concludes he can’t, I think he is the kind of patriotic leader who would not put George Washington move and say it’s"

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: time for someone else."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Hours before the debate in Atlanta,Ossoff led an event with local leaders and small-business owners promoting Biden and Vice President Harris's campaign."I am here to deliver a very simple message: We must reject Donald Trump's comeback,"Ossoff said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: He said small businesses "appreciate competent leadership" that put Main Street at "the center of this administrations “attention."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Ossoff has been relatively quiet since the debate. His office provided a statement from an unnamed aide to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution saying he "fully supports President Biden's reelection and blasted Trump as "the most dangerous presidential candidate" ever.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Schatz, one of the most dynamic senators on social media, has not mentioned Biden's name in the debate concluded.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Here is my best advice re the last 48 hours. If you are gonna stare at your screen all freaked out, then use your energy to do something that will help，"Schatz wrote two days after the debate.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: He then provided a link for liberal activists to volunteer with groups campaigning to elect Senate Democrats, state legislative Democrats and a leading progressive advocacy group.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: There was no link to the Biden-Harris campaign site.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: For a few days after the debate, their campaign embraced a talking point that no longer was needed to call on Biden to step aside before next month's Democratic National Convention in Chicago. But that line fizzled as House Democrats began calling for him to stand down.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Among Schumer's caucus,Sen. Joe Manchin III (I-W.Va.)came closest last weekend, when, as The Post reported, an all-hands- on-deck crew worked to stop him from using one of the Sunday political chat shows to break with the president.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The effort to rein in Manchin, Who formally changed his party registration to independent this year but who still attends caucus lunches, had echoes of the summer of 1998 when congressional Democratic leaders worked feverishly to

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: avoid defections about whether Bill Clinton should resign as the president.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Reporters tracked Joseph L. Lieberman, then a Connecticut Democratic senator who would serve as the 2000 vice- presidential nominee before leaving the party in 2006. Lieberman then was considered a conscience of the Senate and many believed would call for resignation amid revelations about Clinton's affair with an intern.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Such behavior is not only inappropriate," Lieberman finally said in a floor speech. "It is immoral and it is harmful."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But he never demanded Clinton's resignation, nor did any Senate Democrat. At the impeachment trial, every Senate Democrat voted to acquit Clinton.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Like today's situation, House Democrats had less loyalty: 31 voted to formally begin an impeachment trial, and five voted to impeach him.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden and Clinton face vastly different circumstances.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Clinton had been reelected two years earlier,by a wide margin,when voters already had plenty of information about his personal behavior.His approval ratings soared throughout 1998 amid the sex scandal and remained steady in the months after the release of a lurid special counsel report.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden now faces reelection at a time when a large majority of the public questions his ability to do the job,and the debate performance only further confirmed those fears.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: On Sunday just two members of Schumer's caucus-Sens. Chris Murphy(D-Conn.)and Bernie Sanders(I-Vt)-are slated to appear on the political shows.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Like Schatz and Ossoff, Murphy,50, has been a strong Defender of Biden but has spent most of this Senate recess in private. He remained supportive of Biden in a local media interview June 28, but said about the debate performance: "There isn't any sugarcoating it."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Sanders,82, has emerged as one of Biden's most vociferous surrogates. During the debate week, he barnstormed Wisconsin on Biden's behalf. As he told the Associated Press on Tuesday, the president's debate performance might have been“painful" but the alternative is worse.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I'm going to do everything I can to see that Biden gets reelected," Sanders said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: If he is to survive, Biden needs more senatorial supporters like Sanders.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Trump allies prepare to tie Harris to president on vulnerable issues

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: DEMETRUS FREEMAN/THE WASHINGTON POST

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Vice President Harris attends a meeting at the White House April 25. The Trump campaign is seeking to counter any extra appeal Harris may have to women and younger voters if she becomes the nominee.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: GOP attack line to focus on border, 'coverup' on health if Biden drops out

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
BY ISAAC ARNSDORF,
    JOSH DAWSEY
AND MARIANNE LEVINE

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Kamala Harris is not the Democratic nominee for president.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But Donald Trump's campaign is already previewing how it would run against her should the vice president abruptly become the nominee in the wake of President Trump's inauguration, debate performance, as some Democratic officials and strategists have started calling for.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Trump and his allies are escalating lines of attack against Harris, which seek to portray her as further to Biden's left and blame the vice president for the border crisis. They are also introducing a new messaging that accuses her of covering up the state of Biden's health.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Trump-who has previously made fun of Harris's first name and spread false allegations that California-born Harris was a foreigner not eligible for office-is personally enthusiastic about the prospect of running against her, a person familiar with his comments said. He posted a video on Wednesday that showed him calling her “pathetic”and“so f--ing bad." The campaign is pointing to polling showing Harris running similarly to Biden against Trump, possibly weaker with White non- college-educated men who could be key to winning Midwest battleground states

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I think the bottom falls out for Democrats with blue-collar,

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: working-class people in Pennsylvania,Wisconsin and Michigan with Kamala Harris,”said senior Trump adviser Jason Miller,who on Friday circulated years-old clips of Harris saying she would ban plastic straws and re commending people donate to a bail fund that assisted some people charged with violent crimes. "She's viewed as a California radical."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Still,some advisers and allies acknowledged that Harris, 59, could change the race as a more vigorous campaigner with the potential to energize young voters and women. And they said her opportunity to choose a new running mate could further alter the dynamics of the match up,especially if she adds a Midwestern governor such as Josh Shapiro (D-Pa.)or Gretchen Whitmer (D

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
"Kamala Harris is the less likeable and more chaotic face of the Biden-Harris regime."  
Taylor Budowich, 
CEO of MAGA Inc. Super PAC, which dubs Harris the "Invasion Czar”

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Mich.) to the ticket.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "The policy debate doesn't change, the capabilities of the candidate changes—all the problems associated with a declining Biden physically and mentally go away," said Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), a close Trump ally. "If she picks a governor from Pennsylvania or Michigan, that changes the game."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The White House and the

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden campaign have rejected questions about Biden's health and pressure for him to withdraw, but privately advisers acknowledged they have a limited time to reassure his panicking party. Harris spokeswoman Rhyan Lake said: "Vice President Harris is proud to be President Biden's running mate. No matter what false attacks Trump and his extreme allies make, she will continue to defend the Biden-Harris record and prosecute the case against Donald Trump."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Democrats argued that Harris, as a former prosecutor, could be an effective messenger against Trump, who was convicted in May on 34 felonies. They also said she has showed leadership on abortion issues and said that has propelled Democratic wins in recent elections.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Donna Brazile, a former acting chair of the Democratic National Committee, said Harris has already withstood years of withering attacks from Republicans. She noted that Trump has similarly insulted other Black women such as New York Attorney General Letitia James and Fulton County, Ga., District Attorney Fani T. Willis, and she warned that Trump's barrage against the first woman and first Black vice president could backfire.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "They have been throwing paint, rocks, mud and just about every other metaphor I could come up with since the day she was inaugurated... I feel like saying where have you been?" Brazile said. "This is no time for their team to start attacking any woman," she added of Trump, referencing his conviction for paying hush money to an adultfilm actress and jury finding of liability for sexual abuse.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In 2020, Trump spread a base

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: less conspiracy theory that falsely suggested Harris might not be eligible for office, echoing his false allegations about President Barack Obama's citizenship. Harris's parents immigrated from India and Jamaica, and she was born in Oakland, Calif. Trump also made a show of mispronouncing Harris's name.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Trump on Thursday debuted a new nickname for Harris: "Laffin' Harris," making fun of the way she laughs. The campaign has also run an ad mocking Harris's laugh, and a statement from his top advisers on Tuesday called her Biden's "Cackling Copilot."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Trump's team is reemphasizing long-standing criticisms of Harris focused on her 2021 appointment to lead the administration's response to a surge of crossings at the U.S.-Mexico border. The MAGA Inc. super PAC on Wednesday dubbed Harris the "Invasion Czar," a reference to Biden's naming her to oversee his administra

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: tion's handling of the surge of migration at the border.Trump describes the wave of attempted crossings as an "invasion,"using unsubstantiated claims and inflammatory language to dehumanize and vilify migrants.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Kamala Harris is the less likable and more chaotic face of the Biden-Harris regime," said the PAC's CEO, Taylor Budowich. "She wouldn't only widen the map in the presidential race, but would be the nail in the coffin for Democrats' hopes to keep the Senate and win back the House."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Some people close to Trump expressed concern that Harris could take a different approach to Israel's war in Gaza, the source of a damaging fissure in the Democratic coalition.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: While Harris's elevation would eliminate voters' concerns about Biden's ability to serve another four years, Republicans have indicated they would keep the issue alive by accusing her and other

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Democrats of hiding his condition and misleading the public. They will also argue that, if Biden decides he is not fit to run and yields to Harris, he should also remain in the presidency immediately.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: On Thursday, former Trump White House adviser Stephen Miller called for Harris to testify to Congress about her knowledge of Biden's health status. Rep. Chip Roy (R-Tex.) told Fox News on Friday that Harris should be subpoenaed and could be impeached for "lying to the American people" about Biden's mental state and not invoking the 25th Amendment, which provides for a handoff of power in case the president is unable to discharge his duties.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "No one has been more central to the cover-up than Kamala Harris," the Republican National Committee said in an email Friday, citing 16 times Harris has vouched for Biden's fitness.

layout_dets.label: 页眉
layout_dets.text: SUNDAY, JULY 7, 2024 \(\cdot\) THE WASHINGTON POST

layout_dets.label: 页眉
layout_dets.text: EZ RE

layout_dets.label: 页码
layout_dets.text: A5

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: ELECTION 2024

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Debate left Biden team flailing, unable to remedy worsening political narrative

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: JIM VONORUSKA/GETTY IMAGES

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Protesters gather outside in Madison, Wis., where President Biden held a rally on Friday. Following the June 27 presidential debate, Biden's campaign has scrambled to do damage control.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: BIDEN FROM A1

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Knew what they thought they knew about Biden. Polls show that he is losing to Donald Trump, a man who almost never led polling averages until this cycle. The president needed a referendum on his predecessor. But suddenly the race was about Biden. Could he really do the job?

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Rather than take those concerns head-on, Biden followed the speech and rally by retreating from public view—a series of private fundraisers awkwardly using his teleprompter, a retreat with his family to take pictures with photographer Annie Leibovitz, short scripted addresses at the White House—just 32 minutes of combined public comments over five days, none of it off the cuff.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Sentiment on Capitol Hill soured, donors organized against him, and some public polls showed significant erosion. Independent Democratic strategists circulated plans to build up Vice President Harris. His own advisers and staff began to speak out, alarmed by what one called the "deafening silence." Then began the drip-drip of elected and former leaders asking him to step aside.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: By midweek, nothing had been contained—a classic snowball effect. Each new effort only highlighted how much more he needed to do. Belatedly, Biden declared confidence in himself, dismissed the polls, vowed to do more.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I would have been more aggressive if I was them," said Al Sharpton, an ally who has been telling others to stick with Biden. "They needed to have him out earlier, to show there was nothing. The White House seemed surprised at the reaction. They should have fired right back. You don't give your enemies the chance to set your narrative. They let their enemies set the narrative."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: This story, about one of the most consequential weeks of modern presidential politics, is based on interviews with more than three dozen aides, advisers, lawmakers, governors and other Biden allies, most of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations. Together they paint a picture of the Biden team's failure over the past several days to contain a crisis that is tarnishing his legacy and threatens his presidency.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "This Democratic circular firing squad will continue, but it will end," said Dmitri Mehlhorn, a donor adviser to LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman who has been working furiously to rally support for Biden's continued candidacy. "The question is: Does it end in a couple weeks, which is manageable, or does it end in a couple months, which will be a disaster. It's a self-inflicted wound, and the question is: Do we keep shooting ourselves?"

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: One bad night

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Joe Biden showed up late to the biggest test of his 54-year career. He told aides he didn't need the CNN studio tour to show him the camera angles and lights. He had done debates for decades. They insisted anyway.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The motorcade was set to depart the Atlanta Hyatt Regency at 8 p.m., with reporters frantically rushed from dinner into vans. But Biden didn't leave until 27 minutes later, arriving at the studio with less than 30 minutes to spare. He never learned where to look on the split screen when his opponent spoke.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: About 50 million Americans watched him lose his train of thought at times. Democrats watched him miss easy openings to attack Trump, while landing some others. When Trump was talking to him, he sometimes looked confused. His voice was quiet and raspy.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden said later he was tired from international travel 11 days earlier. Aides took responsibility for the pale makeup. He had a problem with him. He had prepared with too much detail. He wasn't really sure.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: One top Biden supporter, who screamed at his television during the event, saw something else. This was a version of the private, frail Biden who had shown up before in small meet-and-greets and mansion fundraisers. "When you are talking to him, it feels like you are talking to grandpa because of his age," the person said. "He is clear, but he is grandpa clear."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: For years, top supporters had been wary of his candidacy, but they respected him too much to intervene. They were proud of his accomplishments. Incumbents tend to be reelected. Biden beat Trump before. They pushed aside

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: the obvious.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
None of it was a state secret.
Biden, 81, had been losing his train of thought in public for years as president. His voice, once bombastic, meandered to mumble. The “fingertip politician” energy of the Barack Obama years had gone stiff and wooden. It was getting worse.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But Biden and his top aides had made these supporters a deal, sometimes explicitly. He would show up, they promised, for a few big moments to put the doubters to rest at the State of the Nation. These, he notes, his nominating convention, some major campaign rallies.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Biden was so confident, he called for a June debate quoting Clint Eastwood — “Make my day, pal,” he told Trump. His campaign started selling cans of water called “Dark Brandon’s Secret Sauce.” The tough talk concealed a remarkably brittle blueprint for, in the words of his campaign,

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Everyone lost confidence by Monday. I started hearing from donors, members, everyone on Monday. It was only getting worse." A Democratic member of Congress said the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: saving American democracy, slowing global warming and preventing World War III.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The mayor of Atlanta, the chairman of the Democratic Party and top Democratic donors gathered at Cooks and Soldiers, a restaurant a few miles from the CNN studios, to watch the debate. They could see right away what was happening. "Sadness" was how one person described the gathering.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: After the debate, Trump was thinking about going to the spin room, but decided against it because Biden did so poorly. "No one was more shocked at Biden's performance than Donald Trump," said one adviser, ready to twist the knife. Afterward, Trump told aides that he couldn't even look at Biden.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Something had been unlocked, the unspoken spoken. Everything was now under a microscope. At a $100 million East Hampton mansion two days later, Biden described a French cemetery at Normandy as Italian. Donors were stunned he spoke so briefly -about six minutes-and left without taking questions.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In New Jersey, at the governor's private villa overlooking the Navesink River, he spoke so softly that a crowd of 50 craned their heads to hear him speak from a teleprompter. Over dinner that night, participants reported a detailed discussion of policy, though Biden was hard to hear and sometimes struggled to complete his thoughts.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Lost days

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: At least 16 senior White House and campaign officials prepped him for the debate over six days at Camp David, the presidential retreat in Maryland. When he returned Sunday to see his family and take photographs, he and his wife were unstaffed as usual, save a single top aide for each.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Some had gone to second homes, some back to Delaware or to see their own families. This

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: was a team that had seen a crisis like this before. They thought they had a handle on it, with memos calling for calm and internal polling showing little change after the debate. The ad featuring the North Carolina rally was cut and debuted on MSNBC's “Morning Joe.”

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But inside, new cracks appeared. Someone began talking to reporters about how the president had been ill-served by some of his top aides in debate prep, prompting Biden to make calls of reassurance to staff. There were whispers about family dissent, which members of the family denied. It was a distraction at a crucial time.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: “That was un-Biden behavior,” said a top adviser later last week. “That is generally not the way this operation has handled these things.”

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: It took days for the team to realize how bad the damage was inside the party. Biden spoke fine from a teleprompter Monday, when he denounced the Supreme Court's ruling on presidential immunity. This was not a polling crisis. It was a political one. The calls were literally coming from inside the House.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "Monday is the day this turned - this has turned," said one Democratic member of Congress. "Everyone lost confidence by Monday. I started hearing from donors, members, everyone on Monday. It was only getting worse."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: It took until Tuesday afternoon for Biden to start contacting Democratic leaders. The only outreach some rank-and-file members received was a Wednesday polling update from Hillary Beard, the Biden campaign's House members director. She wrote that any drop in the polls was "a moment in time, not a reshaping of the race." Campaign volunteer sign-ups had jumped threefold. Ninety-five percent of recent donations came in under $200.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "The talking points suck, totally suck," the member added. "They did a terrible job after the debate. Terrible."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Former House speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), the best vote counter of her generation, knew right away. "I think it's a legitimate question to say, 'Is this an episode or is this a condition?"" she said Tuesday, opening the floodgates. Rep. James E. Clyburn (D-S.C.) called for Biden to do town halls. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) said people need to know that Biden and his team "are being candid with us."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A Wednesday meeting with Democratic governors, demanded by the governors themselves, surfaced more concern. All still publicly supported him, some effusively. But the governors of Maine and New Mexico said their states could be competitive in the presidential race. Colorado Gov. Jared Polis told Biden that people had come to him with a message: Tell Biden to drop out.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Vice President Harris, once an afterthought and a punchline in the party, was enjoying a swell of support, as most party leaders concluded she was the only viable alternative - the only candidate who could claim incumbency and spend the money Biden raised.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In the governor's meeting she found her voice, demanding everyone get behind Biden. "This is about our f---ing democracy," she declared, a prosecutor once again.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Doubling down

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: There is no disagreement among allies about what Biden should do next to stay in the race.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: To me this is just very

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: straightforward. There is a very simple path to this. You just have to go out and do it. If you can't do it, that is a different thing," said Stuart Stevens, the lead consultant for Mitt Romney's 2012 White House bid, who now supports Biden and wants him to stay in the race. "You do town halls and interviews, you do a 72-hour blitz and midnight rally that leaves reporters calling their parents and editors to say, 'I can't do this anymore.'"

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But that sort of endurance was never part of the Biden campaign plan. He doesn't talk or walk like before. He needs more sleep, new shoes, a shorter staircase on Air Force One. In his first press interview since the debate, with a radio station Wednesday in Pennsylvania, his bungled words - nothing new, folks-now circulated like evidence.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Boasting about choosing the first Black vice president, he said "the first Black woman to serve with a Black president." He tried to describe himself as the first

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Catholic to win statewide in Delaware. "I'm the first president to get elected statewide in the state of Delaware," he said instead.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Inside the White House and the campaign, the rank and file tried to keep their heads down. They know how to work hard, with the discipline of a corporate consulting firm. One person described it as a "hold-the-line and throw punches" culture, proud to have overcome party skeptics many times before. But dismay crept out. Had they been misled by the senior staff about his fitness? Campaign pollsters didn't attend the senior staff meetings with the president. Was anyone giving it to him straight?

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A rally Friday in Madison, Wis., showed that the North Carolina speech was no aberration. He could still thunder at a teleprompter. But when he sat for a 22-minute interview with skeptical ABC News anchor George Stephanopoulos, the difference reappeared. Biden has a credible claim to being in command, still making the decisions that matter, understanding the stakes. He has run the country through a time of historic tumult. But he is not the candidate who was part of winning presidential elections three times before.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Talking about how he prepared for the debate, he trailed off again, just like he did before Trump. He said, "I get quoted. The New York Times had me down, at 10 points before the debate, nine now, or whatever the hell it is. The fact of the matter is, what I looked at is, that he also lied 28 times." (The Times poll showed Trump's national lead growing from six to nine points among registered voters after the debate.)

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: At one point, Stephanopoulos asked if he had watched the debate afterward. The president said, "I don't think I did. No."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Billionaire donors, for all their swagger, don't get to order a president around. But a cruel conventional wisdom is setting in. "I'd estimate that for every 10 people who think he should exit, one thinks he should stay," said

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: one donor adviser. The Biden campaign counters that last week was the best grass-roots fundraising start of any month during this campaign.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The campaign, meanwhile, has not been able to answer the central question of their detractors. What is the empirical case for Biden winning when 7 in 10 voters don't think he is up for the job and Trump is sitting on hundreds of millions of dollars to make him look worse than he is? How do you stage a referendum on Trump when another Democrat calls for Biden to drop out every day?

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "President Biden is taking his popular vision to move this country forward to the American people and the voters who will decide this election," Biden campaign spokesman Kevin Munoz said in a statement. "Trump is barely campaigning, and every day whether he's golfing or getting in fights with himself online, he's forced to defend his toxic, losing Project 2025 agenda. Our view is that it is the contrast and binary choice that will matter and determine victory this November."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The House returns to Washington on Monday, and Sen. Mark R. Warner (D-VA.) is looking to rally fellow senators to call for a change. Multiple people publicly vouching for Biden, at the same time calling for the White House and campaign, privately say there's no path.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: His family is still with him. The race is still single digits. And Biden remains hopeful. As he likes to say, America can do anything if its people work together. But not a single thing we can't."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: But in private, people around him have detected some shift. He admits the danger now, can sound more somber at times.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: One person who spoke to him over the Fourth of July holiday said, "I think he is focused on recovering, but I personally think he's still in the denial phase of grief."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Ashley Parker contributed to this report.

layout_dets.text: THE WASHINGTON POST \(\cdot\) SUNDAY, JULY 7, 2024

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Civil right lawyer confronts police force in Miss. town

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: MISSISSIPPI FROM A1

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: she stepped into the back of a police cruiser and traced the journey made by dozens of her clients- some beaten, some accused of infractions as minor as driving without insurancepast the town's Confederate monument, to the county jail.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "I'm going to tell the world what you're doing here," she vowed to Henderson that day in June 2023.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Almost five months later, the head of the U.S. Justice Department's civil rights division stood in the banquet hall of a Lexington church to make an improbable announcement: The agency would aim its mighty investigative resources at Lexington's police force, which at the time had dwindled to about 10 officers and would soon shrink further.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Rural America is guaranteed the same rights as our largest cities, Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Kristen Clarke told those in attendance, some of whom were plaintiffs in the lawsuit. Joseph Jefferson had filed alleging false arrests, excessive force and more.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Similar Justice Department probes have focused on much larger places, such as Minneapolis, Baltimore and Seattle. The agency has also investigated conditions in jails and prisons in Mississippi, a state where multiple local law enforcement agencies have been found to use violence as a tool of policing, and where the Justice Department recently won lengthy sentences for six members of the infamous "Goon Squad" of the sheriff's department in Rankin County, population 157,000.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Lexington, seat of Holmes County, drew the Biden administration's attention mostly because of Jefferson. Twice she went to Washington to lobby officials and lay out her case. She had collected claims of rampant abuses allegedly committed by the small department's chiefs and officers: that they were targeting Black people for prosecution; falsifying or destroying evidence; committing assaults, including of a young disabled woman; and coercing Black women into sex. In one instance, they were accused of pulling a pregnant woman out of her car and throwing her to the ground. The woman said she later suffered a miscarriage.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Jefferson was also struck by an onslaught of relatively mundane abuses: what she describes as a sort of death by traffic ticket.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She first heard about the nighttime police checkpoints, near Black-owned bars and outside events at the predominantly Black high school, during a phone call from a local resident in the spring of 2022. Police would check driver's licenses and make arrests for unpaid fines, the caller said. That led to more fines, jail time and bond, which many of the arrestees could not pay.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The abuse of law enforcement power to maximize municipal revenue gained national attention nearly a decade ago when the Justice Department revealed it in Ferguson, Mo. — as part of an investigation of local police after a White officer's shooting of a Black teenager touched off a debate over race and policing.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In Lexington, a town where about 1 in 6 people are White, 99 percent of those arrested are Black, according to jail logs reviewed by The Washington Post.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Jefferson began meeting with many of them, making weekly trips in her cracked-windshield Mini Cooper from her home in Hattiesburg, 150 miles away, to record their accounts. On behalf of her social justice nonprofit, JULIAN, she mobilized a network of reform-minded lawyers to help represent defendants in Lexington's municipal court.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Jefferson spent two nights in jail after her own arrest, declining to pay the fee for what she saw as an unlawful charge of disturbing the peace, among other counts. Dressed in an orange jumpsuit, she found potential clients among her cellmates — women who described officers pressuring them into sex to avoid arrest. She took notes with a pen, which is forbidden inside the jail but was slipped to her by a kind guard.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: After she got out, local reporters interviewed her in the parking lot of Lexington's library.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "They've been terrorizing Black citizens here," Jefferson said.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: A secret recording

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Sam Dobbins, Henderson's

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: predecessor, was hired as Lexington's police chief in 2021, as residents were complaining about an increase in crime.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: His solution: aggressively police the roads. Officers quickly tripled violations issued for “disturbing the peace” and “following too close,” according to data obtained by the American Civil Liberties Union via public-records request.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: According to officers who have since left the department, Dobbins insisted on having the cars of Black arrestees towed rather than allowing family members or friends to pick up the vehicles — as was once the practice in Lexington, a poor town in the fourth-poorest county in the United States, according to U.S. census data.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
Both Dobbins and Henderson declined interview requests. 
Dobbins did not respond to questions about the towing directive or the financial burden it put on people already struggling to make ends meet.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: For Robert Lee Hooker, who joined the department in 2021, the change in policy crossed a line. Hooker, who is Black, started recording his conversations with the chief.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: One day in 2022, according to a recording reviewed by The Post, Dobbins assured Hooker he would cover for him if Hooker killed "in cold blood." Dobbins used the n-word and a homophobic slur, bragged that he'd killed 13 people in his career, and seemed to relish the notion that Lexington's Black residents feared him, the review showed.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: JULIAN, which by then had also heard accusations of police abuses from several Lexington residents, began lining up lawyers for those who had been arrested or alleged mistreatment, and holding meetings at a community center. Some who spoke up at those meetings have told Jefferson that police later pulled them over, apparently as retribution.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Jefferson talked to residents about suing the department, asking them to trust a justice system that many viewed with suspicion. "I told Hooker he should make his recordings of Dobbins public.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Hooker soon left the department and released the audio via the Mississippi Center for Investigative Reporting, triggering national headlines and outrage. The board of aldermen fired Dobbins in a 3-2 vote, and Henderson was named as his replacement.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Lexington's mayor, Robin McCrory, who is White, declined to be interviewed.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Henderson had joined the department in 2015. While working in Lexington, he held down a second job as police chief in even smaller Goodman, Miss. He left the latter job after being accused of sexually assaulting a woman he arrested in 2019.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text:
Close to half of Lexington's police officers quit after the Dobbins recording was released. 
Once Henderson became chief in Lexington, he tried to bolster the ranks by hiring the inexperienced and untrained.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Again, it was a disgruntled former police officer who blew the whistle.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: A family story

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Jefferson traces her intolerance of racism and her fascination with the law to 1991, when her aunt and grandmother were employed as employees of federal judge Charles Fiecing of Mississippi.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Pickering entered the national spotlight when Senate Democrats filibustered his 2001 appointment to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit. Among their concerns: the judge's personal connections to segregationists and segregationist organizations during the civil rights movement in Mississippi.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The young Jefferson regularly played with Pickering's granddaughter, sometimes running laps around Pickering's estate. One day when Jefferson was 5, she watched from a distance as Pickering delivered a new directive to her aunt and grandmother: Jill could no longer go inside the house unless she was working with them. Jefferson said she didn't socialize with the judge's granddaughter again. Her aunt later told her that she believed Pickering forbade the friendship because his granddaughter was White, and Jill was Black.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Banished to the lawn during Mississippi summer days, Jefferson said, she felt like a "stray dog." Confused and angry, she aspired to someday command

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: “He seemed to be able to navigate the world and make things happen,” Jefferson said. “I wanted to do what he did, but do it to get back at him and other White people who I could tell were racist, even though I didn’t really know what that was then.”

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Pickering, 87, told The Post that Jefferson's accusation about her and his granddaughter was "absolutely not true," though he said he may have discouraged his employees from allowing Jill to interfere with their household work.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Her version of the story remains a foundational memory, however.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Much later, after leaving a corporate law job she found soulless, Jefferson founded JULIAN. It was named for her former husband, the first civil rights leader who was a professor at the University of Virginia, Jefferson's alumna mater, and died in 2015. In addition to representing poor clients, the nonprofit, based in Hattiesburg, investigated and revealed modern-dayynchings in Mississippi.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: At first in Lexington, JULIAN focused on helping to arrange lawyers for criminal defendants who couldn't afford them. Soon, Jefferson felt she had the makings of a lawsuit, and enough evidence to compel a state or federal investigation.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In May last year, 44-year-old Leroy Secherest told JULIAN that police had retaliated against him for interrupting officers who were beating a young, developmentally disabled woman he knew. Secherest said he was driv-

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: ing down Highway 12 when he saw officers punching her.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Days later, after Secherest posted about the alleged assault on Facebook, his son called and said he was being arrested at Lexington's basketball courts. Secherest said he rushed there and Henderson told him: "I've been waiting to catch up with you... Stay out of police business."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Secherest said officers body-slammed him, put him in a choke hold and Tasered him. An arrest report accuses him of possession of a controlled substance, based on a small amount of marijuana police say they found in Secherest's car after entering the vehicle to turn it off. The report also accuses him of disorderly conduct, saying he refused to take his hand out of his pocket and used an "aggressive" tone.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Secherest, who denies being disorderly, spent the night in jail but has not been formally charged or received any notice of a court date. His son was arrested, too; police wrote in Leroy Secherest's arrest report that they found drugs and a gun in the car the son was traveling in.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Jefferson said JULIAN has not yet received footage of Leroy Secherest's arrest from Lexington, which also did not include it in response to public information requests from The Post.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "That's been a consistent problem in this case," Jefferson said. "And we know the reason why - they delete the footage that

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: shows them breaking the law."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Lexington City Attorney Katharine Barrett Riley did not respond to questions about whether the camera was deleted body-camera footage.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The elder Secherest's arrest became a key anecdote in Jefferson's campaign.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She'd already called the Mississippi attorney general's office, which rarely investigates local law enforcement agencies and wasn't required to investigate even fatal police shootings until 2022, but suggested she report her findings to the FBI. Then she emailed and made calls to the office of Gov. Tate Reeves (R). Neither responded to The Post's requests for comment.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Jefferson said she offered several allegations to the local FBI field office. When the FBI declined to investigate, she said, she turned to its parent agency, the Justice Department.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Under President Biden and President Barack Obama, the nation's premier law enforcement agency has launched investigations of dozens of cities for unconstitutional policing since 2009, including New Orleans; Oakland, Calif.; and Louisville. When it finds a pattern and practice of wrongdoing, the civil rights division generally seeks a court-mandated compliance agreement. Justice Department civil rights officials may also recommend that the department's criminal division consider bringing charges.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Some of Jefferson's most powerful allegations came from her interviews with Mactrice Shields, who came forward last summer in a recently ousted Lexington police officer willing to hire her story.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She helped Jefferson understand a puzzle she had been struggling to solve. What motivated Henderson, a Black police chief, to allegedly continue his racist predecessor's discriminatory practices?

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Shields, who was hired by Henderson in December 2022, painted a portrait of a chief drunk on power.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She had moved from Jackson to Lexington that year after getting approved for low-income housing for herself and her tween daughter. On her second day in town, she said, she accidentally ran a stop sign near the police station, and was surprised when the officer who gave her a ticket invited her to stop by the station and apply for a job.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Shields, 31, said Henderson quickly made his intentions clear.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "He said, 'They're gonna like you, but you're mine," Shields recalled.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Henderson nullified the traffic ticket, she said, and invited her to shadow officers. Four weeks later, he hired her. Like several other men in the department, she had not attended a single police academy class.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Arrest logbooks and a trial

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In the summer of 2022, Jeffer

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: son requested records from the Holmes/Humphreys County regional jail of arrests made under Henderson and Dobbins. Instead of a digital file, the warden invited Jefferson into the administrative offices, where she found stacks of leather-bound logbooks listing the names, ages, race and other information of arrestees.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Jefferson photographed page after tattered page of the hand

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: written records with her phone, then catalogued the arrests in an Excel spreadsheet. Portions of the logbooks were unreadable, but Jefferson found that between June 2021 and June 2023, Black people were arrested far more often than White people, even adjusting for their percentage of the population.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: About 40 percent of the arrests of Black people were for minor

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: violations like disregarding a traffic device or no proof of insurance.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "You won't find many White people arrested by Lexington," Barry Rule, the warden, said in an interview. "They stereotype."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Jefferson has filed two federal lawsuits - in August 2022 and January 2024, containing allegations by 22 named plaintiffs against Lexington, its police department and individual officers. Some of the claims were dismissed after the judge reviewed body-camera footage from certain incidents Jefferson said she sought but could not get.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Riley, the city attorney, would not comment on the remaining allegations while the lawsuits are pending.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In all, at least six lawsuits have been filed in federal court against Lexington and its police department since 2019, including one by the ACLU on behalf of a Black

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: woman who claimed she was wrongly arrested by Dobbins and Henderson in 2021. In that case and three others, Lexington submitted denials and claims of immunity from civil penalty under the doctrine of qualified immunity, a legal framework that often protects individual officers.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Since announcing their investigations in November, Justice Department investigators have interviewed Rule, the warden, and much of his staff, as well as many of Jefferson’s clients.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: In February, after Jefferson and several Lexington residents made fresh complaints of unfair pricing, the U.S. Department's Clarke sent a letter to town leaders. She told them that arresting people for unpaid fines with no consideration of whether they had been charged to pay violates the Constitution.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It's time to bring an end to a two-tiered system of justice in

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: our country in which a person's income determines whether they walk free or whether they go to jail," Clarke's letter said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A month earlier, Jefferson had stood trial for her own arrest the previous summer, when she had refused to pay the $35 fee to avoid being jailed for failure to comply, disturbing the peace, resisting arrest and blocking a roadway.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Like many criminal defendants in Mississippi, she faced not a jury of her peers, but an elected judge in Justice Court who is not required to be a lawyer. The Justice Court verdict can be appealed to a higher court for a jury trial, presided over by a jury trial, presided over by a judge who is a member of the state bar.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Jefferson and her attorney laid out her case, one starkly at odds with the government's version of events.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She said she had twice driven by a location where officers had pulled over a car and were questioning the driver. She recorded parts of the encounter on her cellphone. An officer testifying for the prosecution said he initiated contact with Jefferson because he was blocking a roadway, which Jefferson denies.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: As part of her presentation to the court, she read aloud from an affidavit from a former Lexington officer, who was still with the Department in the months before Jefferson's arrest.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: He reported hearing officers talking about finding a way to arrest Jefferson.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Holmes County Justice Court Judge Marcus Fisher, a30-year-old who is Black and is not a member of the Mississippi Bar, found Jefferson guilty of all the charges.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She said she had expected the result in Justice Court and considered not mounting a defense and waiting for her opportunity with a jury, but fought the case anyway as a signal to town residents looking to her for solutions.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "We knew this would be a sham," Jefferson said. "But I don't want the community to think the person fighting for them is just going to give up on fighting for herself."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Local and regional media scrutinized the conviction, and Jefferson received an emailed letter from the court days later. The conviction had been vacated.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: She wondered - for the first time, she said - if Lexington's leaders could be convinced they are not above the law.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: 8 policies that could be vulnerable to challenges

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: AMANDA ANDRADE-RHOADES FOR THE WASHINGTON POST

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: The Supreme Court on July 1. The court's landmark Loper Bright ruling jettisoned a doctrine known as Chevron deference.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: BY JACOB BOGAGE

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Regulations that touch nearly every facet of American life could face new challenges after the Supreme Court's move to overturn a long-standing legal precedent last week. Just days later, litigants and lawyers are already taking aim at some rules with new motions and filings.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The court's landmark ruling in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo jettisoned a doctrine known as "Chevron deference," which generally required courts to defer to the expertise of federal experts when regulations faced scrutiny. The decision — a6-3 vote along ideological lines — jeopardizes federal rules in policy arenas from climate change to low-income food assistance, and tobacco safety to pharmaceutical approvals, and much more.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The precedent dates to 1984, so years of regulations and lower court rulings were made following its lead.Now legal scholars are unsure how much of the U.S.'s administrative framework- decisions made by legions of experts and bureaucrats responsible for the daily operations of the federal government - could fall in the months and years to come.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "It means chaos," said Dorothy A. Brown, a law professor at Georgetown University. This is the Supreme Court cutting back on agency power knowing that Congress can never pass a law that will answer all questions. But it limits what government can do to protect people, protect consumers and impose costs on big corporations."

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Here are eight policy areas that could be overhauled by the Loper Bright ruling.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: 1. Student loan forgiveness

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Hundreds of billions of dollars in student loan assistance could hang in the balance now. The Education Department has promulgated half a dozen rules related to student loan repayment or forgiveness since July 2023, and two of them are the subject of ongoing lawsuits that allege government overreach.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "No policy is at greater risk than the administration's student loan forgiveness efforts, which spend hundreds of billions of dollars without congressional authority." said Michael Brickman, a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: and a former senior adviser in the Education Department under President Donald Trump.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Republican attorneys general in 18 states have sued to stop the Saving on a Valuable Education program, which lowers monthly student loan payments and offers a shorter path to loan forgiveness.They argue that Congress never envisioned anything as expansive as the program in the law underpinning the regulation.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Attorneys for Career Colleges and Schools of Texas made similar arguments in their lawsuit to block the Borrower Defense to Repayment rules,which clears the debts of students whose colleges used illegal or deceptive tactics to persuade them to borrow. The Education Department is enjoined from fully implementing either rule.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The new legal landscape will make it harder for the department to defend its "pro-student" regulations, said Dan Zibel, cofounder of the National Student Legal Defense Network and a former deputy assistant general counsel in the Education Department under President Barack Obama.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: — Danielle Douglas-Gabriel

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: 2. Protections for transgender students

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A new Biden administration regulation protecting transgender students and laying out how schools must respond to accusations of sexual assault and harassment was already being challenged, and the new ruling gives opponents further ammunition to stop it.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The regulation is the administration's interpretation of the half-century-old Title IX law, which bars discrimination on the basis of sex in federally funded K-12 schools, colleges and universities. The administration, citing a 2020 Supreme Court ruling, included discrimination based on gender identity in its definition of sex discrimination, meaning schools might be required, for instance,to allow transgender students to use pronouns and bathrooms that align with their gender identity. The provision was celebrated by LGBTQ+ advocates and derided by conservatives.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The rules, which were set to take effect on Aug. I, have already been temporarily blocked by three different federal courts covering different parts of the country, with

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: additional suits pending.The Biden administration's regulation replaced a similar one written by the Trump administration,which bolstered the procedural rights of the students accused of sexual assault or harassment. It's unclear whether the Supreme Court would now allow either one of the rules to go forward.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Laura Meckler

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: 3. Workers' rights

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Expanded overtime pay eligibility,new requirements for employers to accommodate pregnancy,guidelines on workplace harassment and standards holding franchised brands responsible for labor law violations could all be in jeopardy.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "This has created many, many new areas to litigate," said Ann Lofaso, a professor of labor law at West Virginia University.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Supreme Court ruling almost immediately put a check on the Labor Department's authority.Hours after the ruling came down Friday,a U.S. District Court judge in eastern Texas cited the decision in an order to block the federal overtime expansion from applying to Texas state employees.The rule went into effect Monday and makes millions more workers eligible for overtime pay nationwide But labor and employment attorneys say the Texas judge's decision signals that another court will probably block the rule.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Rules the Labor Department established to implement the bipartisan 2022 Pregnancy Workers Fairness Act, which provides new pregnancy and childbirth related legislation that addresses a number of several pending lawsuits. That includes a case filed by 17 states in April over a requirement that employers provide "reasonable accommodations" for employees seeking abortions. A memo in that regard is also made by the New Supreme Court decision.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Separately, a highly anticipated Labor Department rule introduced this week that would regulate workers'exposure to extreme heat will likely be vulnerable.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "That's ripe for a challenge," said Stephanie Adler-Painidris, a lawyer at the firm Jackson Lewis who represents employers.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: - Lauren Kaori Gurley

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: 4. Electric vehicle support and emissions limits

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Federal government help for

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: electric vehicles - and a federal crackdown on emissions from gasoline-powered cars and trucks - may be in trouble.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Biden administration’s most consequential climate rule could be newly vulnerable: The Environmental Protection Agency’s plan to boost sales of electric vehicles while slashing emissions from gasoline-powered cars and trucks.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Republican attorneys general from more than two dozen states had already sued the EPA over the Biden administration's most consequential climate rule, a sweeping attempt to transform the U.S. auto market. The top trade association for the U.S. oil and gas industry, which could see demand for its products decline as consumers shift to EVs, has also challenged the regulations in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. Opponents say the agency has overstepped its authority.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The EPA will need to convince the court that Congress empowered it to issue the rules, said Jeff Holmstead, a partner at the law and lobbying firm Bracewell LLP and a former top EPA official under President George W. Bush.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: "The question is going to be, 'Did Congress clearly intend to give EPA authority to force a fundamental shift in the transportation sector?'" Holmstead said.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: -Maxine Joselow

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: 5. Corporate climate disclosures

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Publicly traded companies are soon supposed to start sharing key details about their carbon footprints and how much of a threat climate changes poses to their bottom lines. But the Supreme Court's decision may kill that requirement before it even takes effect.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Securities and Exchange Commission, the country's main Wall Street and banking regulator, approved that new requirement in March. The rule tests the powers of the federal government to compel companies to confront global warming, making it significantly harder for businesses to gloss over their role in higher emissions and their vulnerability to climate change. And it immediately came under legal assault; the SEC paused enforcement as soon as multiple lawsuits were filed.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: The major Supreme Court rulings of 2024

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: A look at cases on Trump immunity, abortion pills, social media, guns, Jan. 6 rioters and more.

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: BY ANN E. MARIMOW, NICK MOURTOUPALAS AND TOBI RAJI

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: The Supreme Court ended a historic term Monday that put the justices at the center of many of the nation's most politically sensitive debates, with blockbuster rulings on whether former president Donald Trump is immune from prosecution and on the power of regulatory agencies and the administrative state. Here's a look at the most significant decisions of the term.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Prosecuting Trump for trying to block the 2020 election results

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Trump v. United States

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: ● Joined the majority ● Dissented ○ Decision author

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: LIBERAL BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Limits on social media posts

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: NetChoice LLC v. Paxton, and Moody v. NetChoice LLC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: LIBERAL BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: CONSERVATIVE BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: What they ruled: Former presidents are immune from prosecution for official actions taken while in the White House but do not have immunity for unofficial acts — a broad new definition of presidential power that will upend parts of Donald Trump's criminal cases and add months more pre-trial court hearings.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Why it matters: The decision split along ideological lines and appears to rule out one set of allegations in Trump's federal election interference trial, involving his conversations with Justice Department officials after Joe Biden's 2020 election victory. The looming delays mean that trial almost certainly will not happen before November's presidential election, in which Trump is the presumptive Republican nominee.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: What they ruled: Lower courts must re-examine two laws in Texas and Florida that would have prevented social media companies from removing certain political posts or accounts, to more fully address the First Amendment issues at stake.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Why it matters: The cases test whether state governments or tech companies have the power to set the rules for what content can appear on popular social networks, which play an increasingly central role in political discourse and U.S. elections. The unanimous ruling to block the state laws while litigation continues did not answer that question.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Charging Jan. 6 rioters with obstruction

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Fischer v. United States

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: LIBERAL BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: CONSERVATIVE BLOC

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Power of federal agencies

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, and Relentless Inc. v. Dept. of Commerce

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: LIBERAL BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: CONSERVATIVE BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: What they ruled: Federal prosecutors improperly charged a Jan. 6 rioter with obstructing or impeding an official proceeding, using a statute that the court said must involve impacting "the availability or integrity" of records, documents or other objects.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Why it matters: The ruling essentially says that prosecutors overreached in using the charge against Jan. 6 defendants, since it was created to address document shredding and other fraud after the collapse of the energy giant Enron. Hundreds of charged or convicted rioters can now go back to court to ask for their charge. The charges are also face other charges, or have completed their sentences, but a few dozen could see their bail time reduced.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: The ruling could also affect the Justice Department's stalled federal election interference case against Trump Two of the four charges he faces are based on the obstruction statute.But prosecutors  say those charges should still stand.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: What they ruled: Judges no longer have to defer to agency officials when interpreting ambiguous federal statutes about the environment, the workplace, public health and other aspects of American life.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Why it matters: In issuing its ruling, the court overturned a 40-year-old legal precedent known as "Chevron defiance," long a target of conservatives interested in reining in the power of the administrative state. The court's decision will significantly curtail the power federal agencies have to regulate thousands of private companies, products, industries and the environment.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Homeless encampments in public spaces

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: City of Grants Pass, Ore. v. Gloria Johnson

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: LIBERAL BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: CONSERVATIVE BLOC

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Emergency room abortions

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Idaho v. United States

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: LIBERAL BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: CONSERVATIVE BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: What they ruled: Homelessness is not a status protected by the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment, therefore laws banning homeless people from sleeping in public spaces are prohibited.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Why it matters: Local and state officials are struggling with how to manage the nation's homelessness crisis. Prohibiting homeless encampments is one potential tool, but many jurisdictions do not have enough beds for everyone, and many unhoused people prefer staying outdoors to being in a shelter.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: SEC tribunals

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Securities and Exchange Commission v. Jarkesy

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: LIBERAL BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: CONSERVATIVE BLOC

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Opioid lawsuit settlement

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Harrington v. Purdue Pharma

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: LIBERAL BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: CONSERVATIVE BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: What they ruled: A divided court invalidated the Securities and Exchange Commission's use of in-house legal proceedings to discipline those it believes have committed fraud, saying the reliance on internal tribunals, rather than federal courts, violates the Constitution.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Why it matters: The ruling is another example of the court limiting the power of federal agencies and one of several cases this term challenging the power of the executive branch.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: What they ruled: The justices blocked a controversial Purdue Pharma bankruptcy plan that would have provided billions of dollars to address the nation's opioid crisis in exchange for protecting the family that owns the company from future lawsuits. In a 5-4 decision that scrambled ideological lines, the majority found that the plan was invalid because all the affected parties had not been consulted on the deal.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Why it matters: The closely watched fight involving the maker of OxyContin is part of a national reckoning over the role of drugmakers and other companies in the opioid addiction public health crisis. It split relatives of overdose victims and those whose lives were shattered by opioid addiction.

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: Downwind industrial pollution

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Ohio v. EPA, Kinder Morgan Inc. v. EPA, American Forest & Paper Association. v. EPA, U.S. Steel Corp. v. EPA

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: LIBERAL BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: CONSERVATIVE BLOC

layout_dets.label: 标题
layout_dets.text: White House communicating with social media companies on misinformation

layout_dets.label: 段落
layout_dets.text: Murthy v. Missouri

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: LIBERAL BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: CONSERVATIVE BLOC

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: What they ruled: The court ruled 5-4 to pause the Environmental Protection Agency's ambitious "good neighbor" plan as it is challenged in a lower court. The plan would have limited smog-forming pollutants from power plants and other industrial facilities that cause problems for their downwind neighbors in other states.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Why it matters: The decision is the third time in as many years that the court's conservative majority has curbed the EPA's power to regulate pollution. Those challenging the plan called it unworkable, prohibitively expensive and illegal. The EPA disagreed and said the initiative was needed to protect the health of residents in downwind states, particularly the young and elderly.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Note: The majority opinion was unsigned. Jackson concurred with the majority and also filed a partial dissent.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: What they ruled: While litigation on the issue continues in lower courts, hospitals in Idaho that receive federal funds must allow emergency abortion care to stabilize patients - even though the state strictly bans abortion.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Why it matters: The Biden administration sees this case as one of the few ways it can protect abortion access in states that have banned the procedure since the overturning of \( \text{Roe v. Wade} \) two years ago. Idaho bans abortions unless necessary "to prevent the death of the pregnant woman," while the federal Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act, known as EMTALA, requires hospitals to stabilize or transfer patients from hospital to home. This is not at risk of death. The decision, issued a day after it was prematurely posted on the court's website, is temporary, and does not settle the question of whether the federal law preempts strict state bans.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: What they ruled: The Supreme Court rejected an effort to sharply limit what the White House can say to social media companies about posts the administration believes contain misinformation. A divided court said the Republican attorneys general in Louisiana and Missouri and individual social media users who brought the challenge did not have legal grounds, or standing, to do so.

layout_dets.label: 图注
layout_dets.text: Why it matters: The case gave the Supreme Court an opportunity to shape how government officials interact with social media companies and communicate with the public online. The challengers wanted to bar the Biden administration from pressuring social media companies to remove posts from their platforms that the government deems problematic, accusing the administration of violating the First Amendment by operating a sprawling federal “censorship enterprise.”
